itineraries.title: Grand Tour of Morocco: From Tangier to the Sahara Dunes
itineraries.subtitle: 20 days on the road crossing Morocco from north to south - blue medinas, Saharan desert, earthen kasbahs, Atlantic coast, and imperial cities.
itineraries.notes: Avoid Merzouga in July-August: temperatures exceed 45°C, desert bivouacs inadvisable. Tichka Pass (D12) occasionally closes in winter after heavy snowfall - plan alternative route via Aït Benhaddou directly. Advance booking recommended for desert bivouacs and Jardin Majorelle during high season.
itineraries.climate: Best time: March-May and September-November, with temperatures ranging from 20-28°C on the coast, 15-25°C in the mountains. Avoid July-August: extreme heat in the Sahara (45°C+), Marrakech and Fes sweltering (38-42°C). Winter is mild on the coast but desert nights drop near freezing.

visits.text: Arrival in Tangier and first immersion in the medina: the Grand Socco, former marketplace, marks the crossroads between the colonial town and the old city. The Kasbah, perched atop the medina, houses the Dar el Makhzen - the former sultan's palace converted into a museum, displaying Roman mosaics and ethnographic collections. Climb to the terrace: the view sweeps across the Strait of Gibraltar and, on clear days, the Spanish coastline.

activities.text: Wander the medina's alleys in late afternoon: the souks come alive, the scents of spices mingle with those of warm bread, and shopkeepers close up for the day. This is when Tangier reveals its true character, far from organized tours.

Mint tea at Café Hafa, perched on a cliff overlooking the strait since 1921: generations of writers and artists have set down their notebooks here facing the horizon. Settle on the terrace to watch ferries pass between two continents.

visits.text: 14 km west of Tangier, Cap Spartel is the extreme northwestern point of continental Africa: this is where the Mediterranean and Atlantic meet before your eyes. The lighthouse dates from 1864 - climb to the platform to watch the two seas merge into one. The sight is more impressive than you'd imagine.

5 km from the cape, the Caves of Hercules open onto the Atlantic through a fissure whose shape eerily resembles the map of Africa. The site has been occupied for over 7,000 years BCE - archaeologists found stone tools here. According to legend, Hercules rested here before completing his eleventh labor. Come early morning to avoid the crowds; entry opens at 9am.

activities.text: After the caves, walk along Achakkar Beach at the foot of the cliffs: it's a wild, uncrowded beach where you can stroll along the rocks. A good contrast to the bustle of Tangier's port.

visits.text: Road from Tangier to Chefchaouen through the slopes of the Rif: the first mountain hairpins reveal the red tile roofs and first blue facades long before entering town. Late afternoon arrival recommended to catch the light in the medina.

Place Uta el-Hammam is the heart of Chefchaouen: sidewalk cafés, the Great Mosque with its 15th-century octagonal minaret, and the ochre-walled Kasbah built by Moulay Ali Ben Rachid, founder of the city in 1471. Inside the Kasbah, an ethnographic museum displays costumes, musical instruments, and pottery - climb the tower for views over the medina's blue rooftops from above.

activities.text: First stroll through the blue alleys at dusk. Chefchaouen's blue traces back to the Sephardic Jewish community that arrived from Spain after 1492 - they painted the walls to symbolize sky and the divine. Get lost in dead-end streets without trying to see everything: that's the best plan.

visits.text: The Spanish Mosque (Bouzaafar) is THE viewpoint of Chefchaouen: built in the 1920s during the protectorate but never used for worship, it's now the photographers' essential spot. Allow 25 to 30 minutes walking from Ras el-Maa. Arrive an hour before sunset - the medina shifts from brilliant blue to golden and orange tones as the sun descends behind the Rif ridges.

The Ras el-Maa spring, a few minutes from the medina, is Chefchaouen's natural breathing point: water descends from the mountains, women come to wash laundry, children play on the rocks. It's a scene of daily life worth more than many monuments.

activities.text: For those with energy, the excursion to Akchour waterfalls (30 km from Chefchaouen) is one of the region's most beautiful: natural pools, cedar forest, and the famous Bridge of God, a natural rock formation. Local operators organize shared taxi transfers from the main square.

Tour the artisan souks early morning - wool textiles with Berber patterns, rugs, and the town's signature blue pottery deserve a visit. Monday and Thursday, the local market sets up with farm products at local prices.

visits.text: Road from Chefchaouen to Meknes with a stop at Volubilis, Morocco's largest Roman site: 42 hectares of UNESCO-listed ruins, founded in the 3rd century BCE. At its peak, the city had between 10,000 and 20,000 inhabitants. The Arch of Caracalla (early 3rd century CE), the Villa of Venus mosaics, and the forum are the centerpieces. Go before 10am - after that, the heat is punishing and there's no shade on site.

3 km from Volubilis, the holy village of Moulay Idriss Zerhoun clings to two hills shaped like camel humps. This is the resting place of Idris I, founder of Morocco's first Muslim dynasty and the country's first Islamic king. Every summer, for more than a month, the village hosts the Moussem (pilgrimage) of Moulay Idriss, one of the most important in Morocco.

Meknes, nicknamed the city of the 'Moroccan Louis XIV': Sultan Moulay Ismail made it his capital from 1672 and endowed it with 40 km of ramparts pierced by 20 monumental gates. Bab Mansour, main gate to the imperial city, is one of Morocco's most imposing. The Mausoleum of Moulay Ismail, open to non-Muslims, is a masterpiece of zellige and stucco.

activities.text: Evening stroll through Meknes' medina: less touristy than Fes or Marrakech, it has retained an authentic character with its butchers, grocers, and artisans working in their shops.

visits.text: The Chouara Tanneries of Fes are traditional tanneries still in operation - they work with methods unchanged since the 11th century. You see them from the terraces of the leather shops overlooking the vats: take the sprig of fresh mint the shopkeepers offer you at the entrance to soften the smell. In the morning between 8am and 10am, the dyers are at work and the colors are at their brightest.

The Bou Inania Madrasa, built between 1350 and 1357, is open to non-Muslims. Its zellige tilework, carved cedar woodwork and mashrabiya screens are among the finest examples of Marinid art in Morocco. Allow 45 minutes to explore it at a relaxed pace.

The Nejjarine Fountain and its square are the artisan heart of Fes: cabinetmakers work cedar wood in workshops opening onto the alley, and the Wood Museum housed in the adjacent fondouk displays regional crafts across four levels. The museum's terrace offers a plunging view over the medina's rooftops.

activities.text: Get lost in Fes el-Bali in late afternoon - with its 9,000 alleys, the medina of Fes has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1981 and remains one of the largest pedestrian medinas in the Arab world. A local guide for two hours is recommended for the first day: landmarks are virtually nonexistent for uninitiated visitors.

visits.text: The Al-Qarawiyyin Mosque, founded in 859, is considered the world's oldest university still in operation. Not accessible to non-Muslims, but open doors onto the courtyard allow glimpses of the interior from certain adjacent alleys - a fleeting view sufficient to gauge the place's proportions.

The Mellah, Fes' historic Jewish quarter, contrasts with the rest of the medina through its projecting balconies and different facades. The Ibn Danan Synagogue, restored, can be visited. From the Mellah, the gilded Royal Palace Gates are visible at the end of the grand esplanade - the palace itself is not open, but the entry gates are an essential photo subject.

Borj Nord, a 16th-century fortress perched on the hill above the medina, houses the Arms Museum and above all offers the best panorama over Fes el-Bali - the medina sprawls across both valley slopes, with its rooftops, minarets, and the green mass of the Al-Qarawiyyin Mosque at center. See it in late afternoon for the light.

activities.text: Moroccan cooking class: operators offer morning classes in medina riads - tagine, pastilla, briouats, and mint tea. A 3-hour morning that lets you leave with verified recipes.

visits.text: Road from Fes to Merzouga via the Ziz Valley and Midelt: the route crossing the Tizi n'Talrhmt pass (1,907 m) is one of the most spectacular passages in the Middle Atlas. As altitude descends, vegetation disappears and the ochre and red tones of the pre-Sahara take over. Arrival in Merzouga early afternoon.

First contact with Erg Chebbi in late afternoon: the dunes stretch 22 km long and 5 km wide, with peaks reaching 150 m. It's one of the most imposing dune systems in the Moroccan Sahara. Sunset transforms the golden sand into a palette of red, orange, and violet - climb the nearest dune to the village to watch the transformation.

activities.text: Camel ride to a bivouac in the open desert: local operators offer 1.5 to 2-hour round-trip packages by camel to reach a camp at the foot of the great dunes. Berber dinner, percussion music around the fire, and night under the stars. It's an experience that requires advance planning - book through your Merzouga riad or guesthouse upon arrival.

practical_info.booking: Book same day or day before

visits.text: Sunrise from the summit of a dune: wake before dawn (allow 20 minutes minimum climbing) to be in place when light begins grazing the dune crests. The contrast between shadow and light on the waves of sand is the most photographed moment in the Moroccan Sahara. After sunrise, the desert's silence reclaims its dominion.

Lake Dayet Srij, at the dunes' edge, is a seasonal lake that forms after rains and attracts flamingo colonies. Depending on season, birds are visible to the naked eye from the shore. The village of Khamlia, a few kilometers from Merzouga, is inhabited by a Gnawa community whose percussion music is played evenings.

activities.text: Quad or 4x4 in the dunes during morning: operators offer one- or two-hour circuits through Erg Chebbi's secondary dunes, with access to zones usually inaccessible on foot. The experience is radically different from camel riding.

visits.text: Stop in the Dadès Gorges en route from Merzouga: the pink limestone cliffs close in on the road until forming a vertiginous corridor. At the gorges' entrance, the 'monkey fingers' - rock formations eroded into grotesque bulbs - are one of the strangest landscapes in pre-Saharan Morocco. Allow 30 to 40 minutes.

The ksar of Aït Ben Haddou, 30 km from Ouarzazate, has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1987. This fortified village in pisé and raw earth, built from the 17th century on the trade route between Sudan and Marrakech, has served as a backdrop for some twenty Hollywood films - Gladiator, Game of Thrones, Lawrence of Arabia. Climb to the collective granary (agadir) atop the ksar for panorama over the Ounila Valley.

activities.text: Dinner on a terrace in Ouarzazate facing the Atlas: the city, at 1,160 m altitude, marks the frontier between mountains and desert. The Draa Valley palm groves begin here.

visits.text: The Kasbah Taourirt, built in the 19th century for the powerful Glaoui tribe, dominates Ouarzazate from downtown. A section is open for visits: stucco-decorated apartments, interior courtyards, and terraces offer a glimpse of Berber luxury of the era. Allow 45 minutes.

Excursion south into the Draa Valley: from Ouarzazate, the valley stretches for 200 km through palm groves, pise villages and kasbahs. The road first crosses the Jbel Saghro by the Tizi n'Tinififft pass, then reaches the valley at Agdez: from there the finest landscapes begin - palm trees, market gardens, and kasbahs appearing at every bend in the road. Allow a full-day round trip from Ouarzazate.

activities.text: Visit the Atlas Studios of Ouarzazate: one of the world's largest open-air filming complexes, used since the 1960s for productions from Lawrence of Arabia to Babel. Guided tours access sets still standing - Jerusalem, Rome, or Egyptian ruins in papier-mâché amid the desert. It's kitschy but fascinating.

to_next_leg.road_type: mountain pass

visits.text: Drive from Ouarzazate to Marrakech via the Tichka pass (2,260 m): it is the highest pass on Morocco's national road. The climb is long and the hairpins are many - the landscapes change radically with each altitude. At the top, stop for the view over both sides of the Atlas. Allow 3.5 to 4 hours of driving.

Arrival in Marrakech mid-afternoon. First approach to the medina's ochre ramparts, 19 km long and dating from the 12th century - they give the city that characteristic tint earning it the nickname 'red city'. Settle into a medina riad for total immersion.

activities.text: First evening on Jemaa el-Fna square: at nightfall, the square transforms into a permanent spectacle - storytellers, snake charmers, Gnawa musicians, orange juice stands, and smells of grilled skewers. It's been UNESCO-listed as intangible cultural heritage since 2001. Arrive at 7pm to watch the square gradually come alive.

visits.text: The Koutoubia Mosque, built in the 12th century by the Almohads, is one of North Africa's largest mosques with its 70 m minaret - the model for Seville's Giralda. Not accessible to non-Muslims, but the surrounding gardens offer an unobstructed view of the entire tower. Morning recommended for light.

The Bahia Palace, built in the late 19th century by Grand Vizier Si Moussa, extends across 8 hectares of gardens, interior courtyards, and decorated apartments. Its name means 'the brilliant' - the painted cedar ceilings, mosaics, and moucharabiehs justify the appellation. Visit is self-guided, allow 1 hour.

The Saadian Tombs, rediscovered in 1917 beneath a layer of plaster, house the sepulchers of 66 members of the Saadian dynasty including Sultan Ahmad al-Mansour (died 1603). The main hall, decorated with 12 Carrara marble columns, is a jewel of Hispano-Moorish art. Arrive at opening (9am) to avoid the line.

activities.text: Dive into Marrakech's souks: each street has its specialty - leather, spices, babouches, brass, carpets. The dyers' souk (Souk des Teinturiers) is most spectacular, with wool skeins hanging from facades in red, yellow, and violet. Bargaining obligatory and advised with a smile.

visits.text: The Majorelle Garden, created from 1923 by a French painter and purchased in 1980 by a couturier who saved it from destruction, is Morocco's most visited garden. The intense cobalt blue of the structures - christened 'Majorelle blue' - contrasts with the green of bamboos and cacti. Book online: capacity is limited and queues without reservation are long from 10am. Arrival at opening recommended.

The fashion and art museum adjacent to Jardin Majorelle traces the history of a great French couture house through its archives, sketches, and a selection of iconic pieces. The building's architecture in ribbed red brick is itself remarkable.

Marrakech's Mellah, historic Jewish quarter adjacent to the royal palace, preserves ancient synagogues and distinctive architecture with its overhanging balconies. The Lazama Synagogue, from the 16th century, is the most accessible and best preserved.

activities.text: Traditional hammam in late afternoon: medina hammams offer the complete package - steam, scrubbing with kessa glove, black beldi soap, and argan oil massage. Allow 1.5 hours. A way to close two days of walking through the souks.

visits.text: Arrival in Essaouira and first walk on the ramparts: the former Mogador was built in the 18th century following plans inspired by Vauban's military architecture, at the request of Sultan Mohammed ben Abdellah. The Skala de la Ville, a 200 m crenellated esplanade facing the Atlantic, is armed with some twenty 18th-century Spanish bronze cannons. Atlantic wind is permanent - bring a windbreaker even in summer.

Essaouira's medina, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2001, is laid out in a grid - unlike the labyrinth of Fes or Marrakech, you can navigate easily. Streets smell of thuya sawdust: artisans carve this fragrant wood into objects, boxes, and furniture. The fishing port remains active: go at noon to choose your fish from the stalls and have it grilled on the spot.

activities.text: Sunset on Essaouira beach from the ramparts: the beach extends several kilometers south of town and powerful winds make it a world-renowned windsurf and kitesurf site. Even without practicing, watching kitesurfers evolve at sunset with the walls behind is a spectacle in itself.

visits.text: The Skala de la Kasbah, the medina's oldest quarter (18th century), is accessed through a small door leading to a walkway overlooking the port. From here the bronze cannons protected the port entrance - artillery pieces over 3 m long could launch cannonballs 1,000 m. A unique view over the Purpuraires Islands and fishing boats.

The Bayt Dakira Museum traces Essaouira's Judeo-Moroccan history, a city that was long a center of coexistence between Muslims, Jews, and Christians. Essaouira's Jewish community played a vital commercial role - the recently restored and opened museum is one of the town's most interesting visits.

activities.text: Horseback or camel ride on the beach south of Essaouira: local operators offer one-hour walks at water's edge, with the town's ramparts as backdrop. A way to see Essaouira from the beach.

Grilled fish lunch at the port: choose your fresh fish from the ice-filled stalls - sea bream, sole, shrimp, or sardines - and it's grilled immediately before you. A typical port experience, in an atmosphere of fish market and charcoal smoke.

visits.text: Road from Essaouira to Agadir along the Atlantic coast: argan trees appear shortly after Essaouira - it's one of the rare places in the world where these trees grow, and goats climbing their branches to eat the fruit are an authentic spectacle (not staged, unlike certain tourist spots). The argan forest is a UNESCO biosphere reserve.

The Kasbah of Agadir Oufella, perched on a hill 236 m above the bay, is the only vestige from before the 1960 earthquake that destroyed the city in 15 seconds. The view from the summit sweeps the entire Bay of Agadir, its 9 km beach, and the Souss mountains behind. The drive or walk up is worth the trip.

activities.text: Stroll through Souk El Had: 6,000 shops on several levels, spices, textiles, leather, fruit and vegetables. It is a local market, not a tourist market - prices are displayed and there is less pressure than in Marrakech.

visits.text: Souss Massa National Park, created in 1991 between Agadir and Tiznit, extends across 33,800 hectares of coastal cliffs, dunes, wetlands, and steppes. The Oued Massa estuary is a Ramsar site of international importance for migratory birds: on the 5 km walking circuit, you'll observe flamingos, spoonbills, gray herons, cormorants, and - if you're lucky - the northern bald ibis, one of the world's most threatened species with 95% of the wild population nesting here. Binoculars recommended.

The town of Tiznit, 90 km south of Agadir, is known for its medina ringed by 7 km of pink ramparts and for its silversmiths - the town is Morocco's main center of Berber jewelry. Place du Méchouar and its blue spring are the quiet heart of the old town.

activities.text: 4x4 circuit in the park's animal reserves (Rokein and Arrouis): addax with long horns, dorcas gazelles, scimitar oryx, and red-necked ostrich - species extinct in the wild in Morocco and reintroduced here since the 1990s. Visits are mandatory with a park guide.

practical_info.booking: Guide mandatory, arrange at park entrance

visits.text: Rabat is not on the road from Agadir: the city is about 87 km from Casablanca, 1 hour's drive north, and is visited as a round trip from Casablanca. The Hassan Tower, an unfinished 12th-century minaret, was meant to be the minaret of the largest mosque in the world according to the Almohad sultan Yacoub al-Mansour. His death in 1199 halted the work at 44 m - half the planned height. The 200 columns of the never-completed mosque now form a silent field of stone around the tower.

The Mausoleum of Mohammed V, facing the Hassan Tower, houses the tombs of King Mohammed V, architect of Morocco's independence, his son Hassan II, and Prince Moulay Abdallah. Built between 1961 and 1971 by 400 Moroccan artisans, its green-tiled pyramidal roof, white Italian marble, and zelliges make it a masterpiece of contemporary Moroccan art. Entry is free and open to non-Muslims.

The Kasbah des Oudayas, a 12th-century Almohad fortress on the Bouregreg estuary, dominates the river and Atlantic. Its blue and white alleys resemble a miniature Chefchaouen. Café Maure, inside the kasbah, is the place for mint tea facing the estuary.

activities.text: The Chellah, 2 km from central Rabat, combines Roman vestiges of the ancient city of Sala Colonia (1st century) and a 14th-century Marinid necropolis in a garden invaded by storks nesting on the minarets. A historic monument since 1920 and UNESCO heritage since 2012, it's one of Morocco's most unusual sites.

visits.text: The Hassan II Mosque, built over the sea between 1987 and 1993, is one of the largest mosques in the world, with its 210 m minaret. Its prayer hall can hold 25,000 worshippers, with a further 80,000 people on its esplanade.

Casablanca's downtown Art Deco quarter, built during the French protectorate (1920s-1950s), concentrates one of the world's most remarkable Art Deco architecture collections outside Miami. Place Mohammed V, with its fountains and arcades, is the center. Walk among facades ornamented with geometric forms and Moroccan motifs reinterpreted in concrete.

activities.text: Guided tour inside the Hassan II Mosque for non-Muslims: official providers offer organised tours in the morning and afternoon. Book ahead, places are limited.

Seafood lunch on the Corniche of Casablanca before departure: the waterfront, stretching from the port to Ain Diab, is lined with fish restaurants with terraces on the Atlantic. A final image of Morocco facing the ocean.

seo.h1_title: Grand Tour of Morocco: From Tangier to the Sahara Dunes
seo.intro_paragraph: From Tangier and its mythical caves to the 150 m dunes of Erg Chebbi, this 20-day grand tour covers Morocco in all its diversity: millennial medinas of Fes and Marrakech, pisé kasbahs of the pre-Saharan south, Atlantic coast of Essaouira and Agadir, and natural parks where the world's last northern bald ibises nest. The route follows a logical loop from north to desert, then back up the coast to Casablanca.
seo.seo_hook: Blue medinas of the Rif, 150 m Saharan dunes, UNESCO-listed kasbahs, Atlantic coast, and imperial cities - all of Morocco on a single route.
featured_list: Chefchaouen: the blue town clinging to the Rif mountains since 1471
Merzouga: the dunes of Erg Chebbi reaching 150 m in the heart of the Sahara
Aït Ben Haddou: the pisé ksar listed as UNESCO heritage and backdrop for 20 Hollywood films
Essaouira: the Atlantic Mogador, Vauban-style medina listed as UNESCO heritage since 2001

Souss Massa Park: world's last refuge of northern bald ibis with 95% of wild population

itineraries.title: Morocco’s Atlantic Coast in 8 Days, from Rabat to Taghazout
itineraries.subtitle: Follow the Atlantic coast from Rabat to Taghazout in 8 days, taking in Portuguese fortresses, an oyster lagoon, and surfing.
itineraries.notes: Hassan II Mosque can only be visited at set times: choose a morning tour so you can reach Azemmour and El Jadida before dark, as driving at night is not recommended in Morocco. Along the entire coast, Atlantic breakers make swimming dangerous outside sheltered areas, and most beaches have no lifeguards.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: April through June and September–October, with highs of around 21 to 27 °C from Rabat to Agadir. In summer, the coast stays mild, with daytime temperatures around 21 to 22 °C in Essaouira, but strong winds blow there. Avoid November through January in Rabat, the rainiest months (80 to 94 mm of rain per month).

visits.text: Walls painted blue and white line the narrow streets of the Kasbah of the Oudayas, the citadel overlooking the mouth of the Bouregreg River. Enter through Bab Oudaia, a gate carved between 1195 and 1199 for Sultan Yacoub el-Mansour of the Berber Almohad dynasty. In the 17th century, Moriscos, Muslims expelled from Spain, settled here and founded a republic of privateers that attacked merchant ships. Rue Jamaa leads to the semaphore platform, a former station that sent signals to ships. Come early, before the tour groups.

More recent than it looks, the Andalusian Garden of the Oudayas was created between 1915 and 1918. This was the beginning of the Protectorate, the period when France administered Morocco (1912–1956). With its bougainvillea and citrus trees, the garden imitates those of Al-Andalus, medieval Muslim Spain. Nearby Café Maure offers a chance to take a break on the terrace. Save this garden for the middle of the day, between the kasbah and the medina.

Rabat’s medina, the old city surrounded by ramparts, is best explored without a fixed plan. Its Rue des Consuls, laid out in the 17th century, housed major merchants and foreign delegations until 1912. Farther along, Souk as-Sabbat is nicknamed the street of shoes. To the southwest, the Mellah was the neighborhood where Jewish families traditionally lived. Allow 1 hour to wander: the Kasbah of the Oudayas is just a few minutes away on foot.

Though unfinished, Hassan Tower is even more impressive than a completed minaret. Sultan Yacoub el-Mansour began construction in 1196 for an enormous mosque, but work stopped when he died in 1199. The tower reaches 44 m, instead of the planned height of more than 60 m. Inside, ramps replace stairs: the muezzin, the man who calls people to prayer, was meant to be able to ride up on horseback. The rows of columns in front mark the prayer hall, ruined by the earthquake of 1755. From the center, allow 30 minutes for the uphill walk, or take a petit taxi.

If you enjoy ceremonies, watch the royal guards on horseback outside the Mausoleum of Mohammed V: they generally agree to be photographed. Completed in 1971, this white marble monument with a green roof was designed by Vietnamese architect Cong Vo Toan. It houses the tombs of Mohammed V, a hero of independence, his son Hassan II, and Prince Moulay Abdallah. Non-Muslim visitors view the tombs from an interior balcony. Cover your shoulders and knees; the tourist office lists weekday opening hours as 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.

Chellah brings together two eras across 7 hectares above the Bouregreg River. Below, Sala, an ancient Roman city, preserves the remains of its forum, a temple, and a triumphal arch. Higher up lies the Marinid necropolis, the cemetery of a dynasty that ruled Morocco during the Middle Ages. Enter through a gate completed in 1339. Storks nest on the minaret. Eels live in a pool: according to a local belief, feeding them helped women have children. Following restoration, the site reopened in 2024: 70 dirhams, or 120 with an audio guide.

You will visit Hassan II Mosque in Casablanca with a guide. Built from 1986 to 1993, partly over the ocean, it has a 210 m minaret. The roof of its prayer hall opens in five minutes. The tour takes you through the prayer hall, the minaret hall, and the ablution hall, with its 41 fountains. Tours depart at 9 a.m., 10 a.m., 11 a.m., noon, and 3 p.m., with an additional 4 p.m. tour from mid-March to mid-September, and fewer departures on Fridays. Foreign adult admission: 140 dirhams.

activities.text: A laser installed at the top of Hassan II Mosque’s minaret lights up in the evening and points toward Mecca, with a range of 30 km. Around the building, the esplanade can accommodate 80,000 worshippers, in addition to the 25,000 in the prayer hall. Walk around the ocean side: the mosque rests on foundations of concrete and blocks of rock, facing the waves. Half an hour is enough before getting back on the road south.

practical_info.tip: Required attire for the tour: covered shoulders and clothing extending below the knees; no shorts or tank tops. Remove your shoes and carry them.

visits.text: Ochre ramparts overlook a slow-moving river: Azemmour’s medina lines the left bank of the Oum Er-Rbia. The Portuguese occupied it from 1513 to 1541. Estevanico, a native of the city who had been enslaved, left in 1527 with a Spanish expedition to North America. He was one of four survivors out of several hundred men. Today, many walls display murals, portraits, and calligraphy by Moroccan and foreign artists. Wander without a set route, camera in hand.

activities.text: The Oum Er-Rbia estuary begins just a few minutes from Azemmour’s medina. Wetlands, dunes, and green riverbanks attract migratory birds, and a few fishermen still practice traditional fishing here. Come late in the day to photograph the river, then get back on the road: El Jadida is only about twenty minutes away.

practical_info.tip: Early morning and late afternoon offer the most beautiful light on the river and ramparts.

map_keywords: Portuguese City of Mazagan El Jadida

visits.text: In El Jadida, walk along the citadel that houses the Portuguese Cistern: its interior is closed for restoration and cannot be visited. This chamber, approximately 34 m on each side and supported by 25 pillars, may have served as an arsenal before becoming a water reservoir in 1541. Before the closure, a thin layer of water covered the floor and reflected the vaults. A shaft of light fell through a round opening that once collected rainwater. Orson Welles filmed a scene here for his Othello, released in 1952. Stay outside the construction site.

Next, you will climb a steep ramp onto the ramparts of Mazagan, the former Portuguese name for El Jadida. About 8 m high and 10 m thick, they have a 2 m-wide wall walk. The star-shaped fortress dates from 1541–1548, and UNESCO listed it in 2004. The Portuguese left in 1769: the empty city was nicknamed “the ruined one,” then renamed El Jadida, “the new one,” in the 19th century. From the Bastion of the Angel, the view stretches over the ocean and harbor.

The Sea Gate, at the end of the Portuguese city’s main street, is the old passage where ships unloaded their goods. Beneath a nearby arch, a communal oven still bakes bread brought by women from the neighborhood. Near the entrance, the Church of the Assumption is built in the Manueline style, the Portuguese Gothic style of the early 16th century. The Grand Mosque, right next door, has a five-sided minaret. Ask before photographing local residents at the oven.

Calm water on one side, Atlantic breakers on the other: Oualidia’s lagoon is protected from the ocean by a sandbar. At low tide, the water recedes and sandy islets emerge. The beach along the lagoon offers sheltered swimming areas, and Moroccan families come here for their summer vacations. Stay on the lagoon side: facing the ocean, the shore break—the first waves near the shore—is dangerous even in mild weather.

Oualidia takes its name from Sultan El Oualid of the Saadian dynasty, who had a kasbah built in 1634 to defend the entrance to the lagoon. Along the waterfront, a palace built around 1940 for the future King Mohammed V now stands abandoned. It still belongs to the royal family, however. You can view its arcaded galleries from the beach. Take this short walking loop in the late afternoon, after your swim.

activities.text: “Oysters taste best when eaten right in the water,” says an Oualidia guide quoted in the Moroccan press. Oyster farming was introduced here in 1956. Pacific oysters are raised in beds recognizable by their wooden stakes. Beach shacks serve the oysters raw, with lemon. They are also the town’s main export.

practical_info.tip: The lagoon is sometimes subject to temporary public health restrictions, as in 2024: check locally and buy packaged oysters with a health label from an authorized seller.

activities.text: If you visit between fall and spring, Oualidia’s lagoon fills with birds arriving to spend the winter or stopping along their migration routes. It is part of the Sidi Moussa-Oualidia Ramsar site, a wetland protected by an international convention since 2005, where 114 species of waterbirds have been recorded. Small boats follow the shores, where you can see gray herons, spoonbills, egrets, and flamingos stopping between Spain and Senegal.

practical_info.tip: In spring, when birds are most easily disturbed, ask the boat operator to keep their distance.

activities.text: You can also explore Oualidia’s lagoon at your own pace in a kayak or on a stand-up paddleboard rented on the beach. Sheltered by the sandbar, the water stays calm, which is reassuring for beginners. On the ocean side, a beach shack also rents surfboards. Go in the morning, when the beach is quieter.

practical_info.tip: Check the tide times: at low tide, sandbars emerge and may force you to carry your kayak or paddleboard.

visits.text: It is best to visit Safi’s National Ceramics Museum before Potters’ Hill: you will then understand what you are looking at. The museum occupies the Kechla, a fortress listed as a historic monument, and its terrace offers views over the city. Its seven rooms trace Moroccan ceramics from prehistory to the end of the 20th century, from the Rif Mountains to the High Atlas. One room honors Boujemaa Lamali, a master potter associated with the pottery school that opened in Safi around 1920. Open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.; closed Tuesdays.

activities.text: Earthen kilns and their chimneys rise across Safi’s Potters’ Hill, visible from the Bab Chaaba gate at the edge of the medina. This neighborhood, listed as a historic monument since 1920, houses cooperatives where artisans mainly preserve traditional techniques. Safi is renowned for its blue ceramics. Walk among the workshops and watch the potters throw pots—that is, shape clay on a wheel.

practical_info.tip: If a potter invites you to watch them work, leave a tip of around 20 dirhams or buy a piece.

visits.text: Beginning in 1760, French engineer Théodore Cornut designed part of Essaouira’s medina for Sultan Sidi Mohammed ben Abdallah. The city combines European-style ramparts with Arab-Muslim architecture, earning it UNESCO World Heritage status in 2001. Its port, oriented toward sub-Saharan Africa, long earned it the nickname “Port of Timbuktu.” In late June, the Gnaoua Festival fills the city. Dedicated to Gnaoua music, a Moroccan musical tradition, it also welcomes jazz and reggae: book your accommodations early.

Climb onto the Skala de la Kasbah, the cannon-lined rampart on the medina’s northwestern side: a row of old cannons still points toward the ocean. The platform, accessible at any hour, is a meeting place for the city’s young people. Essaouira’s ramparts served as a filming location for season 3 of Game of Thrones, depicting the fictional city of Astapor. Visit before sunset if you want to enter Bab Ljhad, the northern bastion, which closes at that time.

Blue boats packed along the docks and fishermen mending their nets: Essaouira’s fishing port is first and foremost a working harbor. Carpenters still build wooden boats here, sold throughout Morocco and as far away as France. Sardines and conger eels make up most of the catch. In the market hall at the port entrance, watch the fish auction. Go in the morning, then continue to the Skala du Port, right next door.

There are no signs or audio guides: the Skala du Port, an 18th-century fortified battery, is worth visiting for its cannons and views. From the Borj el-Barmil corner tower, you can see the port and the Mogador Islands, about 1.5 km offshore. These islands form a nature reserve where Eleonora’s falcons, birds of prey, come to breed. In antiquity, King Juba II had purple dye produced here from shellfish. Expect to pay around 60 dirhams; open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. The wind is often stronger in the afternoon.

Bayt Dakira, the “House of Memory,” tells the story of Jewish life in Essaouira, a city where Muslims, Jews, and Christians have lived side by side since its founding. It is in the former mellah, the Jewish quarter. Inside are the restored Simon Attias Synagogue, Torah scrolls, silver Hanukkah lamps (for the Jewish Festival of Lights), marriage contracts, and photographs from the 19th and 20th centuries. King Mohammed VI visited in January 2020. Admission is free; closed Saturdays. Clothing that provides coverage is recommended.

activities.text: More interesting than the souvenir stalls, the woodworking shops built into the space beneath the Skala de la Kasbah let you see Essaouira’s artisans at work. They carve thuya, a local conifer whose root wood is used. This craft has been practiced in the medina for centuries. You can watch the wood progress from a rough stump to a finished object.

practical_info.tip: Compare prices at several workshops before buying.

activities.text: When the wind blows, as it often does, Essaouira Bay fills with kitesurfing kites. The city is nicknamed the “City of Trade Winds,” after the steady winds that sweep this coast. Partly sheltered by the Mogador Islands, the bay is suitable for beginners: several schools offer kitesurfing, windsurfing, surfing, and stand-up paddleboarding. For your first session, choose a school that provides supervision from the beach and has a rescue boat.

practical_info.tip: Stand-up paddleboarding is possible year-round in light winds. Keep a windbreaker handy on the beach.

visits.text: A golden sand beach stretching as far as the eye can see and a white tomb facing the ocean: Sidi Kaouki takes its name from this marabout, the tomb of a local saint. Every August, a moussem, a festival honoring the saint, brings this small Berber village 25 km south of Essaouira to life. The rest of the year, the atmosphere remains peaceful despite the surf schools. Swim with caution: the ocean here is often rough, with strong currents.

activities.text: In Sidi Kaouki, you will find schools renting boards and wetsuits for beginners and experienced surfers alike. The beach break works almost year-round, with the biggest swells arriving in winter. Suitable for beginners, it works best around high tide. From September to March, conditions are better for surfing. From April to October, the steady wind tends to attract kitesurfers and windsurfers.

practical_info.tip: If you’re not surfing, book a horseback ride on the beach with one of the village stables, preferably at sunset. Children enjoy camel rides.

visits.text: More than 500 m on a single wave: that’s possible in Imsouane Bay when the swell comes from the right direction. This fishing village has a point break, a wave that consistently forms in the same place and peels along a rocky headland. The bay’s slow, steady wave suits beginners and longboards. The faster wave at La Cathédrale is for experienced surfers only. The bay works best from low to mid tide.

activities.text: Imsouane’s small harbor still relies on fishing: the village boats supply the fresh fish sold on-site. It’s a good stop on the road between Essaouira and Taghazout to watch the surfers and stretch your legs. Allow about 1 hour 15 minutes for the onward drive to Taghazout.

practical_info.tip: The swell is most consistent from fall through spring; summer is still an option for learning.

visits.text: Locals call the rock at the end of the beach south of Taghazout Imouran, meaning “the dying”; it is also nicknamed Devil’s Rock. According to oral tradition, fighters killed battling the Portuguese in the 16th century are said to have been buried there. This Berber fishing village, 19 km north of Agadir, saw hippies arrive in the late 1960s, followed by surfers. The beach stretches for about 7 km to the rock: set out early if you want to walk its length.

Anchor Point, 3 km north of the village of Taghazout, is a long wave that peels along a rocky headland. With a good swell, it continues as far as the Hash Point surf spot and ends on Panoramas Beach. Conditions are best from September to April. Even if you’re not surfing, settle on the rocks to watch the surfers, keeping out of their way.

activities.text: Take your first surf lesson in Taghazout, where schools and rental shops line the village. To get started, choose a sandy beach over a rocky point like Anchor Point: the bottom is less dangerous if you fall. The region’s waves are best from September to April. Allow half a day for travel, getting equipped, and the lesson.

practical_info.tip: Ask whether the wetsuit and transportation to the surf spot are included in the lesson price.

activities.text: To find out where argan oil comes from, visit a production workshop around Taghazout: alongside fishing and tourism, it is one of the village’s sources of income. The argan tree grows wild in southwestern Morocco. The know-how associated with it, passed down mainly by women, has been on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list since 2014. The fruit is harvested and dried, the pits are cracked, and the kernels—the seeds inside—are ground before the paste is kneaded with warm water.

practical_info.tip: The oil is used in cooking, cosmetics, and traditional medicine: specify your intended use before buying.

to_next_leg.road_type: P1001 road toward the mountains

visits.text: A paradise that depends on rain: in summer, the river in Paradise Valley runs low and the greenery fades. This valley along the Tamraght River (locally, rivers are called oueds), in the foothills of the High Atlas, is lined with palm trees and clear pools where you can swim. From the parking lot, an easy trail reaches the pools in about 30 minutes. Ideally, visit in late winter or early spring, when the river is full.

activities.text: You can extend your Paradise Valley walk by following trails that climb above the cliffs along the Tamraght River. Wear shoes with ankle support and bring plenty of water. Avoid jumping from rocks into the pools when the water is low: accidents have happened here. To continue to Imouzzer des Ida Outanane, plan a round-trip drive from Paradise Valley, followed by a walk to the waterfalls. In this village perched at 1,250 m, the falls flow mainly from January to March.

practical_info.tip: Stalls at the valley entrance serve vegetable tagines and Berber omelets. In Imouzzer, the souk takes place on Thursdays.

activities.text: Agadir-Al Massira Airport, about 20 km southeast of downtown Agadir, serves as the arrival point for this itinerary and connects it to many European cities. From Taghazout, allow for a drive of around 40 km. Agadir itself was almost entirely rebuilt after the earthquake of February 29, 1960.

practical_info.tip: If your flight leaves late, the cable car that opened in 2022 connects Tildi Bridge to Agadir Oufella, the old kasbah, which overlooks the bay.

seo.h1_title: Morocco’s Atlantic Coast in 8 Days, from Rabat to Taghazout
seo.intro_paragraph: Over 8 days, this road trip follows Morocco’s Atlantic coast from the Kasbah of the Oudayas in Rabat to the waves of Taghazout, near Agadir. Along the way, you visit the Hassan II Mosque in Casablanca, the Portuguese ramparts of Azemmour and El Jadida, Oualidia’s oyster lagoon, and the potters of Safi. Two nights in Essaouira give you time to explore the ramparts and harbor before heading to the surfing beaches of the south.
seo.seo_hook: The Kasbah of the Oudayas, Hassan II Mosque, El Jadida’s cistern (closed for restoration), Oualidia’s oysters, and Essaouira’s ramparts: Morocco’s Atlantic coast in 8 days.
featured_list: Rabat: the Kasbah of the Oudayas and Hassan Tower, unfinished since 1199
Casablanca: a guided tour of the Hassan II Mosque, built partly over the ocean
El Jadida: the Portuguese Cistern where Orson Welles filmed Othello; interior closed for restoration
Oualidia: boat rides, kayaking, and oysters on a sheltered lagoon
Safi: the National Museum of Ceramics and Potters’ Hill
Essaouira: a UNESCO-listed medina, fishing harbor, and a bay swept by trade winds
Sidi Kaouki and Imsouane: surfing and waves running for more than 500 m
Taghazout: surf lessons, argan oil, and the pools of Paradise Valley

places_taglines.MA::rabat: Morocco’s capital, with a kasbah, medina, and UNESCO-listed sites.
places_taglines.MA::casablanca: Hassan II Mosque, built partly over the Atlantic Ocean.
places_taglines.MA::azemmour: A medina with ocher ramparts above the Oum Er-Rbia River.
places_taglines.MA::el-jadida: Formerly Portuguese Mazagan, with a star-shaped fortress and vaulted cistern.
places_taglines.MA::oualidia: A lagoon sheltered from the ocean, known for its oysters and birds.
places_taglines.MA::safi: A city of potters and the world’s leading sardine port in the 1950s and 1960s.
places_taglines.MA::essaouira: Formerly Mogador, with a fortified medina facing the islands and the wind.
places_taglines.MA::sidi-kaouki: A Berber village, a long, wild beach, and a saint’s white tomb.
places_taglines.MA::imsouane: Fishing village known for its long, consistent wave.
places_taglines.MA::taghazout: Fishing village that has become a gathering place for surfers north of Agadir.
places_taglines.MA::vallee-du-paradis: Valley of palm trees and natural pools on the road to Imouzzer.
places_taglines.MA::agadir: City rebuilt after 1960, with an airport offering departures to Europe.

Casablanca: Hassan II Mosque and its 210 m minaret
El Jadida: Portuguese Cistern with 25 pillars, within the city inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2004; interior closed for restoration
Oualidia: protected lagoon, oysters farmed since 1956, and waterbirds
Essaouira: UNESCO-listed medina, cannon-lined skalas, and fishing port
Taghazout: waves from September to April and Paradise Valley

itineraries.title: Southern Morocco in 10 Days: Erg Chigaga and Tafraoute
itineraries.subtitle: Over 10 days, follow the Drâa to the dunes of Erg Chigaga, then cross the Anti-Atlas from Tata to Tafraoute and Taroudant.
itineraries.notes: The night at Erg Chigaga is spent at an organized desert camp, with a 4x4 and driver taking you from M'Hamid, where your rental car stays parked. Stay on paved roads, never drive at night, and before departure read the Morocco page of the French government's travel advice, which places the southern stretch of the Algerian border under heightened vigilance.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: October through April, with highs in Ouarzazate ranging from 17 to 27 °C and cool nights, around 2 °C in January. Avoid June through August: average highs exceed 35 °C in Ouarzazate, and temperatures in Tata can exceed 45 °C. Pack warm clothes for nights in the desert, and aim for February to see Tafraoute's almond trees in bloom.

visits.text: It is best to start with the Taourirt Kasbah: it helps you understand all the earthen fortresses of southern Morocco. In the 19th century, the Glaoui family, powerful caïds (local governors), expanded it. It then overlooked the meeting point of several valleys, including the Drâa and Dadès valleys. Its walls are made of rammed earth, soil compacted between wooden boards. Only a small restored section is open to visitors: look up at the woven reed ceilings. Allow 1 hour.

The Ouarzazate Cinema Museum opened in 2007 in a former film studio, directly across from the Taourirt Kasbah. You can walk among sets, props, and filming equipment used in movies shot in the region. Visit it right after the kasbah without getting back in the car: the two entrances face each other.

“Ouarzawood” is the nickname of Atlas Studios, which opened in 1983 west of Ouarzazate on the road to Marrakech. Martin Scorsese's Kundun and scenes from Gladiator are among the productions filmed here. The guided tour takes you through outdoor sets, built to last for the duration of a shoot, and through the workshops. Tours depart several times an hour: come in the early afternoon, then continue to Aït-Ben-Haddou.

to_next_leg.road_type: N9 toward Marrakech

visits.text: Ochre earthen houses stacked up to the top of a hill: the ksar of Aït-Ben-Haddou looks like a movie set, and it has often served as one. This fortified earthen village, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, appears in Lawrence of Arabia, Gladiator, and the series Game of Thrones. Only a few families still live here. Most residents have settled on the other side of the Ounila River, which runs alongside the ksar: cross it using the pedestrian bridge completed in 2011.

If you still have energy after exploring the narrow streets, climb to the agadir crowning the hill of Aït-Ben-Haddou. This former fortified granary protected the entire village's harvests; only its walls remain. From the summit, the view stretches across the Ounila Valley and the ksar's terrace rooftops. Wear sturdy shoes, as the earthen steps are uneven, and head down before nightfall to return to Ouarzazate, about 30 kilometers away.

to_next_leg.road_type: N9 via Tizi n'Tinififft Pass

visits.text: You will cross Tizi n'Tinififft Pass, at an elevation of 1,660 m, on the road from Ouarzazate to Agdz. From the viewpoint, you can see the arid Saghro Mountains, almost devoid of vegetation. The road then descends toward the first palm groves of the Drâa Valley, which begins at Agdz. Stop at the pass for 15 minutes to take in the contrast between the dry rock and the green ribbon of the palm grove.

The Caïd Ali Kasbah overlooks Agdz from a rocky promontory. This 19th-century fortified residence, built of unfired earth bricks, belonged to the caïd, the local governor. Inside, a maze of rooms leads up to the terraces. The building is largely abandoned and belongs to the caïd's descendants: speak with them on-site to arrange a visit.

“Meeting place” is the meaning of Tamnougalt in Tachelhit, the Amazigh (Berber) language of southern Morocco. This ksar, 6 km from Agdz on the other side of the Drâa, was the capital of the Mezguita, the tribe that dominated this part of the valley. Its caïds lived in the Kasbah of the Caïds: three levels of rammed earth surrounding a courtyard, with painted wooden ceilings and carved plasterwork. Some rooms are fragile, so ask before entering. Hire a guide to explore the covered lanes and the former Jewish quarter.

activities.text: In the shade of the date palms in the Agdz palm grove, water flows through seguias, small open-air irrigation channels. They distribute water among plots of henna, mint, and fig trees. Paths connect the douars, the hamlets scattered throughout the palm grove. Set out in the morning with a local guide: they will show you how water flows from one garden to the next and may be able to arrange tea in a local home.

practical_info.tip: The walk is most pleasant in spring and fall; in summer, set out early.

activities.text: If you are in Agdz on a Thursday, set aside 1 hour for the souk, the weekly market where people from neighboring villages come to sell goods and stock up. Spices, dates, and olives fill the stalls, while the butchers occupy a separate area. This is no tourist market, but part of everyday life in the valley. Come in the morning, before the intense heat.

practical_info.tip: The Agdz souk takes place on Thursdays.

to_next_leg.road_type: N9 along the Drâa Valley

visits.text: A 13th-century Quran copied onto gazelle skin is the centerpiece of the library at the Naciria Zawiya in Tamegroute. A zawiya is the headquarters of a Sufi brotherhood, part of a mystical tradition within Islam, and also serves as a place of teaching. This one dates back to 1575 and still holds several thousand manuscripts on medicine, mathematics, and astrology. Access depends on the caretaker being present: ask in Zagora before setting out, and put your camera away, as photography is generally prohibited.

activities.text: No two pots are quite the same green: in Tamegroute, the shade of the glaze, a coating that turns glassy during firing, varies with the heat of the kiln. The village potters still fire their pieces in traditional kilns, and local tradition traces this craft back to Fez. Step into a workshop to watch the pottery being thrown, then compare the shades before buying. On Saturdays, the village souk also displays their pottery.

practical_info.tip: Tamegroute’s weekly souk takes place on Saturdays.

activities.text: You will see your first dunes a few kilometers south of Tamegroute, at Tinfou. They are much smaller than those of Erg Chigaga, but offer enough sand for a first barefoot walk. Stop for half an hour in the early afternoon, then set off again to reach M’Hamid before nightfall: driving at night is discouraged in Morocco.

practical_info.tip: Do not drive at night: the French government’s travel advisory for Morocco advises against it.

to_next_leg.road_type: N9, the last paved stretch before the desert

visits.text: “M’Hamid of the gazelles”: the name M’Hamid El Ghizlane recalls the gazelles that once lived on the nearby plains. The last oasis along the Drâa before the desert, it was long a stop for caravans crossing the Sahara. Several ksour, fortified earthen villages, lie hidden in its palm grove, including M’Hamid Bali and Ouled Driss. Most are almost empty and crumbling. Ask before entering a house: some require a small contribution.

The modest ruins of Ksebt El Allouj in M’Hamid are worth visiting mainly for the history they evoke. They are generally dated to the Saadian dynasty, which ruled Morocco in the late 16th century, when the oasis depended on trade across the Sahara. No one knows exactly what the building was used for. Make it the destination of a short walk through the palm grove, with a local resident as your guide.

activities.text: You will leave your rental car in M’Hamid El Ghizlane, where the N9 ends. The 50 to 60 km leading to Erg Chigaga consist entirely of unpaved tracks across stony plateaus, ancient dry lake beds, and soft sand where vehicles easily get stuck. Book a 4x4 with a driver and an overnight stay at an organized desert camp, a tent camp run by a tour operator, in advance. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours for the journey.

practical_info.tip: Never set out alone on the track in a rental car: the route is unmarked, and windblown sand can erase tire tracks.

activities.text: The sand begins right at the edge of M’Hamid El Ghizlane: small dunes are within walking distance or a short dromedary camel ride away. At sunset, their crests turn orange as the palm grove falls into shadow. It is a good warm-up before Erg Chigaga. Set out an hour before sunset and return before it is completely dark.

practical_info.tip: Temperatures are best suited to dune outings from October through April.

to_next_leg.road_type: Sandy and stony track, 4x4 with a driver

visits.text: Erg Chigaga is Morocco’s largest erg, a sea of sand dunes. It stretches for around 40 kilometers between Jbel Bani to the north and the hamada, a stony plateau, toward M’Hamid. Some dunes rise more than 50 m high. Until around 1990, this was a military zone, and few travelers came here. Even today, there are no roads or villages, only camps. Bring a warm jacket, as nights are cold even after a scorching day.

activities.text: Climb a large dune in Erg Chigaga an hour before sunset. Take your time: in soft sand, every step takes much more effort than it would on a trail. From the summit, the dunes’ shadows stretch eastward, and the silence is almost complete. Keep a headlamp handy for the descent, and locate the camp lights before night falls.

practical_info.tip: Bring at least one liter of water per person for the climb.

activities.text: Slow, swaying, and a little hard on the back, a dromedary camel ride is still the most fitting way to experience Erg Chigaga. You can even reach the erg from M’Hamid on a multiday trek with a caravan. For a first experience, a one-hour ride from camp is enough. Request it when booking your desert camp stay, and wear long pants for greater comfort in the saddle.

practical_info.tip: Book the ride at the same time as your desert camp stay.

activities.text: With no villages for tens of kilometers around, Erg Chigaga’s night sky is dark enough to photograph the stars. The organized desert camp, a tent camp set up by a tour operator, provides dinner and sleeping accommodations. Before booking, ask how the camp manages water and waste: in such a dry environment, it matters. If possible, choose a date near the new moon, when the sky is darkest.

practical_info.tip: Days are hot and nights are cold: bring warm layers.

activities.text: If you get up half an hour before dawn, you will see Erg Chigaga’s dunes turn from gray to pink, then gold. The morning sand is still cool and holds the tracks left overnight by small desert animals. Walk for an hour before breakfast, then pack your bag for the return trip by 4x4 to M’Hamid, where your car awaits.

practical_info.tip: The return trip by 4x4 to M’Hamid takes about 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours.

to_next_leg.road_type: Track by 4x4 to M’Hamid, then paved N9

visits.text: “Timbuktu 52 days”: Zagora’s famous sign showed how long it took to reach this city in Mali across the Sahara, on foot or by dromedary camel. The original has been replaced by a mural, but the old sign still exists. Stop for a photo as you enter town: it is the most evocative reminder of the caravan era.

Amezrou Kasbah is worth a detour precisely because people still live there. In Zagora’s palm grove, you enter through a maze of narrow streets where families live. The path leading there follows a canal shaded by palm trees. Be discreet and do not photograph residents without their permission.

activities.text: Hike up Jbel Zagora, the mountain overlooking the city, on a 3.8 km loop. Allow nearly two hours for about 250 m of elevation gain over rocky terrain, with white arrows marking the way in places. At the foot of the mountain stand the remains of a fortress built by the Almoravids, a medieval Berber dynasty. Set out early and bring water: from the summit, at 966 m, the view takes in Zagora and the Drâa palm grove.

practical_info.tip: Zagora’s weekly souk takes place downtown on Sundays.

to_next_leg.road_type: Paved N12

visits.text: Foum Zguid means “the mouth of the Zguid wadi”; a wadi is a desert watercourse. This small oasis town in Tata Province marks the transition from the Anti-Atlas to the Sahara. Walk in the shade of its palm grove, then visit the remains of the old kasbah on the outskirts. On Thursday mornings, the weekly souk brings the main street to life.

activities.text: You can watch carpet weavers, leatherworkers, and jewelers at work at Foum Zguid’s craft center, which opened in 2022. The town is also the closest to Iriqui National Park, established in 1994 to protect desert wildlife. Its lake, usually dry, filled within a few days after heavy rains in October 2024. No paved road leads there: access is via a dirt track and requires a 4x4 with a driver.

practical_info.tip: Foum Zguid’s souk takes place on Thursday mornings.

visits.text: The water is salty, yet palm trees grow all around: the Tissint waterfalls tumble over rocks in the heart of the oasis. You can swim here to cool off; keep your sandals on, as the wet rock is slippery. The village’s name is also familiar to scientists. In July 2011, a meteorite that fell 48 km to the south was identified as a piece of the planet Mars, thanks to gases from the Martian atmosphere trapped inside the rock.

Disguised as a Jewish traveler, French explorer Charles de Foucauld stayed in Tissint while exploring Morocco. His account, Reconnaissance au Maroc, published in 1888, earned him the gold medal of the Société de géographie. A village guide can take you to his poorly maintained house, about 400 m downstream from the spring. The route passes through the old village’s covered alleys, sheltered from the sun.

to_next_leg.road_type: N12 at the foot of Jbel Bani

visits.text: Built from local earth, Tata’s ksour blend into the landscape. These fortified villages of rammed earth recall the city’s past as a caravan crossroads. Tata’s workshops keep basket weaving, carpet weaving in warm colors, and local pottery traditions alive. Wander through them in the morning before temperatures rise: in summer, they can exceed 45 °C.

activities.text: Beneath the Agadir Lhena palm grove, north of Tata, water flows through khettaras, underground channels that bring groundwater to the gardens. A water clock, or clepsydra, is still used to divide irrigation time among the plots: each family receives water for a measured period. To get there, turn left just after the ford, the crossing through the wadi, drive to the end of the village, then continue on foot along the palm grove trail.

practical_info.tip: Take your time to understand the khettara system: a resident can explain it to you.

activities.text: Climb to the highest point in the village of Agadir Lhena for a sweeping view of the Tata oasis. Palm groves line the Tata wadi, a tributary of the Drâa, at the foot of Jbel Bani, the long rocky ridge bordering the southern Anti-Atlas. A series of oases stretches from Agadir Lhena to Tiguisselt. Go up in the late afternoon, when the light is softer and the heat has subsided.

practical_info.tip: Sunset over the palm grove is the best time of day in Tata.

to_next_leg.road_type: Mountain road toward Tleta Tagmoute

visits.text: Residents call it the “village bank”: the agadir of Aït Kine, a fortified communal granary a ten-minute drive from Tleta Tagmoute, still stores barley, dried fruit, and valuable documents. Archives document its use as early as 1708. Each family has its own room, 76 in total, plus a room reserved for the tribe. A caretaker opens the door at dawn and closes it at sunset: come during the day and ask him for a tour.

activities.text: Park upstream from the Tleta Tagmoute oasis and continue on foot: the seguias, small irrigation canals, guide you from one plot to the next. Pomegranate and olive trees grow beneath the date palms, with grains, vegetables, and alfalfa for livestock in their shade. This layered planting protects the lower crops from the scorching sun. Allow forty-five minutes for the walk.

practical_info.tip: Leave your car upstream from the oasis: explore the palm grove’s paths on foot.

to_next_leg.road_type: Winding mountain road

visits.text: At an elevation of about 1,700 m, Igherm is an Anti-Atlas crossroads where the roads from Taroudant, Taliouine, and Tafraoute meet. An agadir, a fortified communal granary, survives on the edge of town, although rebuilding has altered its form. Stop for tea in the center before taking the narrow road down to Tafraoute.

to_next_leg.road_type: Narrow Anti-Atlas road with a long final descent

visits.text: In 1984, Belgian artist Jean Vérame painted blue a group of large granite boulders rounded by erosion, south of Aguerd Oudad, near Tafraoute. The colors have faded over time, and most of the rocks have since been repainted. The blue contrasts with the pink granite and pale sand. Come early in the morning: the low-angle light brings out the colors, and the heat is still bearable.

Pink granite mountains surround Tafraoute, a small Anti-Atlas town at an elevation of about 1,000 m. Its name comes from the Amazigh word tafrawt, meaning “basin” and, by extension, “valley.” In the center, a small market sits on a knoll overlooked by a minaret, amid renovated lanes. The town is liveliest on Wednesday, the main market day.

activities.text: Walk south from Tafraoute toward the village of Aguerd Oudad, overlooked by a granite rock nicknamed Napoleon’s Hat: its silhouette resembles the emperor’s bicorne, a two-pointed hat. The path follows a dry riverbed to the painted rocks. Farther on, vegetation takes over the riverbed: head back up to the small road at that point. Allow a good two hours and wear closed-toe shoes.

practical_info.tip: From September to May, temperatures are suitable for walking; in summer, set out at dawn.

activities.text: Tafraoute bills itself as the capital of the Berber babouche, a round-toed leather slipper that is often brightly colored. Shops in the center sell them alongside amlou, an almond and argan oil spread that is a regional specialty. Taste the amlou on a piece of bread before buying. For babouches, try several sizes and take your time bargaining.

practical_info.tip: In February, the almond blossom festival brings Tafraoute and the valley to life.

to_next_leg.road_type: Paved R107 to the entrance to the gorges

visits.text: Gdourt, in the Aït Mansour Gorges, is known for its tightly clustered rammed earth houses clinging to the mountainside above the palm grove. In fall, the palms bear dates; in January–February, the almond trees bloom. Greet residents before photographing them, and stay on the paths, as the gardens are cultivated.

activities.text: At the bottom of an arid red-rock canyon, the Aït Mansour Gorges shelter a palm grove that stays green year-round. Allow two hours to walk along the stream, among date palms, almond trees, and olive trees watered by seguias. In 2018, the FAO, the United Nations food agency, recognized the argan-based agriculture of Aït Souab and Aït Mansour as a globally important agricultural heritage system. The road is paved as far as the entrance to the valley; beyond that, the dirt road may require a 4x4.

practical_info.tip: After rain, do not take the dirt road without a 4x4: return via the paved road.

visits.text: The Oumesnat Traditional House is a former family home turned living museum in the Ammeln Valley, about 6 km from Tafraoute. Arranged on several levels around a central kitchen, it shows how local people lived in the 18th and 19th centuries. The owners often lead the tours, which have an admission fee. To get there, leave the main road and follow the dirt road toward Jbel Lekst and the signs for “Maison Traditionnelle.”

Oumesnat’s lanes climb the mountainside between rammed earth houses, some partly carved into the rock. Higher up, the ruins of the old village crumble on the slope. In January–February, almond trees bloom all around. After visiting the Traditional House, climb through the lanes before getting back on the road to Taroudant.

activities.text: Take one of the trails starting in Oumesnat, such as the “Lion’s Head” loop. This name refers to the rocky flank of Jbel Lekst, a 2,359 m peak with the Ammeln Valley stretching out at its foot: seen from a particular spot on the road, it forms the shape of a lion’s head. The trail offers sweeping views of the valley, which has about twenty Berber villages. Bring water and sturdy shoes, as the slopes are steep.

practical_info.tip: To climb Jbel Lekst itself, hire a local guide.

to_next_leg.road_type: Anti-Atlas mountain road

visits.text: Taroudant’s kasbah, the former royal quarter in the northeast of the city, was built in the 17th century by Sultan Moulay Ismaïl. Enter through Bab Sedra, its old gate, to explore a quiet residential neighborhood. Near Bab el Kasbah, you can climb onto the ramparts for a view over the city. In the evening, residents stroll through the park in front of the kasbah.

Mint tea on a café terrace and street performers in the late afternoon: Assarag Square is the heart of Taroudant. Between it and Talmeklat Square, the covered lanes of the craft souk bring together potters, jewelers, coppersmiths (artisans who work with copper), and carpet sellers. Take time to compare before buying, and always negotiate the price.

The smell reaches you before the sight: the Bab Targhount tannery processes hides just outside Taroudant’s ramparts. Around forty tanners prepare sheep, goat, and dromedary camel hides as visitors watch. Nearby shops sell bags, poufs, and sandals made on-site. Hold a mint leaf under your nose if the smell bothers you.

activities.text: Take a horse-drawn carriage ride around Taroudant’s ramparts late in the day, when the sun warms the ocher walls. These 7.5 km of earthen walls date mainly from the 16th century and the Saadian dynasty. They have earned the city its nickname, “Little Marrakech.” Agree on the price before getting in: the hourly rate is negotiable.

practical_info.tip: You can also follow the ramparts by bike or on foot, preferably at sunset.

activities.text: Few souvenirs, plenty of life: Taroudant’s Amazigh souk, the municipal market, mainly sells spices, dried fruit, and household goods. In its open-air section, artisans turn old tires and plastic into saddles, watering troughs, and baskets for donkeys. Enter from Assarag Square. Watch without getting in the way, and ask before taking photos.

practical_info.tip: On Sunday mornings, another souk takes place outside the ramparts to the north, selling livestock and mountain produce.

to_next_leg.road_type: N10 through the Souss Plain

visits.text: On February 29, 1960, at 11:40 p.m., an earthquake destroyed Agadir and killed between 12,000 and 15,000 people, about a third of its residents. Agadir Oufella Kasbah, a fortress built by the Saadian sultans in the 16th century, collapsed that night. Restored since 2020, it can be explored along wooden walkways that follow the course of the old lanes, with audio guides in French. Allow about 50 minutes; the site is open from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

More than a market, an entire neighborhood: Agadir’s El Had souk covers 13 hectares and brings together thousands of stalls behind its 13 gates. It is easy to get lost among the aisles. Make a note of which gate you enter through, and plan your visit for late morning, before heading up to the kasbah.

activities.text: You will ride up to Agadir Oufella Kasbah on the cable car inaugurated in 2022, a 1.7 km line starting at Tildi Bridge. Walkers may prefer the maintained 2.8 km trail. The hill, 236 m above the port, overlooks the entire Bay of Agadir. Go up in the late afternoon to enjoy the light over the ocean.

practical_info.tip: The kasbah site is open from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

activities.text: More than 10 km of sand line the bay, with a waterfront promenade running along Agadir Beach. After the oases and mountains, this is the place to end your trip with a walk facing the Atlantic Ocean. The present-day city was rebuilt about 1.6 km farther south after the 1960 earthquake. Walk toward the port at sunset, keeping the kasbah hill in sight.

practical_info.tip: Al Massira Airport is about 23 km from the city.

seo.h1_title: Southern Morocco in 10 Days: Erg Chigaga and Tafraoute
seo.intro_paragraph: This 10-day itinerary starts in Ouarzazate, follows the Drâa Valley down to M’Hamid, and includes a night at a desert camp in the dunes of Erg Chigaga. It then follows the oasis route to Tata, crosses the Anti-Atlas to the pink granite of Tafraoute, and ends in Agadir after a visit to the ramparts of Taroudant.
seo.seo_hook: Ouarzazate’s kasbahs, the Drâa palm groves, a desert camp at Erg Chigaga, Tafraoute, and Taroudant: southern Morocco in 10 days.
featured_list: Ouarzazate: Taourirt Kasbah, expanded by the Glaoui in the 19th century
Agdz: the ksar of Tamnougalt, former capital of the Mezguita
M’Hamid El Ghizlane: the last oasis of the Drâa, at the end of the N9 road
Erg Chigaga: Morocco’s largest erg, accessible only by unpaved track
Zagora: the caravan sign reading “Timbuktu 52 days”
Tagmout: the communal granary of Aït Kine, in use since at least 1708
Tafraoute: the rocks painted blue by Jean Vérame in 1984
Agadir: Agadir Oufella Kasbah, left in ruins by the 1960 earthquake

itineraries.title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah
itineraries.subtitle: Explore the medina of Fez, its madrasas, its tannery, the Mellah, and Borj Nord over 2 days on foot and by petit taxi.
itineraries.notes: In the car-free medina of Fez, you get around entirely on foot: bring comfortable walking shoes and a map downloaded for offline use. Plan this weekend trip for a Saturday and Sunday, since the Al Batha Museum closes on Tuesdays, Borj Nord on Mondays, and the Bou Inania Madrasa closes for longer on Fridays for congregational prayer.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: March through May and October through early November, with highs of 20 to 26 °C. Avoid July and August, when average highs reach 35 °C. From November through January, the rainiest months, nighttime temperatures drop to around 4 to 8 °C: bring a warm jacket and shoes with good traction.
specialties: Artisanat du cuir et du cuivre

visits.text: It looks very old, but Bab Bou Jeloud, the grand western gate of the medina of Fez, dates from 1913. The French administration built it as a ceremonial entrance. Its ceramic tiles are blue on the outside and green on the inside. Through the arch, you can already see the minaret of Bou Inania, the religious school you will visit next. Unlicensed guides often wait here. If you want a guide, hire an official one: they must show you their Ministry of Tourism ID. Agree in advance on the price, the route, and a “no shops” rule.

visits.text: From floor to ceiling, no wall is bare in the Bou Inania Madrasa, a religious school that housed its students. At the bottom is zellige, a mosaic of small, colorful ceramic tiles; above it is carved plaster; higher still is carved cedar. Sultan Abu Inan of the Marinid dynasty had it built from 1350 to 1355. It is the only madrasa in Morocco that also served as a congregational mosque for Friday prayer. Its prayer hall, reserved for Muslims, can be seen from the courtyard. Admission is 20 dirhams; it closes during prayers, with a longer closure on Fridays.

activities.text: “The Great Climb”: that is what Talaa Kebira means, the sloping street linking Bab Bou Jeloud to the heart of the medina of Fez. There are no cars here: the medina is one of the largest urban pedestrian zones in the world. Goods travel on donkeys or handcarts, so give them the right of way. Farther down, look for the mosaic-decorated minaret of the Chrabliyine Mosque. Shops nearby still sell traditional shoes. Take your time wandering and compare prices before buying.

practical_info.tip: Download an offline map before you leave. If you get lost, make your way to Talaa Kebira or neighboring Talaa Seghira, “the Little Climb”: both link Bab Bou Jeloud to the heart of the medina.

visits.text: As early as 1711, traveling merchants slept upstairs at the Nejjarine fondouk and stored their goods on the ground floor. A fondouk was a merchants’ inn built around a courtyard. Since 1998, the building has housed the Nejjarine Museum of Wooden Arts and Crafts. Inside, you will see carved doors, musical instruments, and wooden tablets made by students at the Quranic school. In the courtyard, the large scale was used to weigh goods. The museum is open from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Finish at the rooftop café, with views over the medina’s roof terraces.

to_next_leg.justification: The two sites are a short walk apart in the medina of Fez: the routing engine returned a null value; the current walk of 0.15 km in 3 minutes is correct.

visits.text: If you see passersby ducking under a beam across the alley, you are approaching the Moulay Idriss II zawiya. A zawiya is a shrine built around a saint’s tomb. These beams mark the boundary of the holy site: until 1912, non-Muslims and pack animals were not allowed to pass beyond them. The tomb belongs to Idriss II, who ruled from 807 to 828 and is traditionally considered the founder of Fez. The interior is reserved for Muslims: approach the doors without photographing worshippers.

to_next_leg.justification: The two sites are a short walk apart in the medina of Fez: the routing engine returned a null value; the current walk of 0.15 km in 3 minutes is correct.

visits.text: Small but exquisite, the Al-Attarine Madrasa may be the day’s loveliest surprise. Allow 30 minutes to visit. Its name comes from the adjacent Al-Attarine souk, the spice and perfume market. The Marinid sultan Abu Said Uthman had it built from 1323 to 1325. Look at the bronze-clad cedar entrance doors: they are copies, since the originals are preserved at the Al Batha Museum. Upstairs are around thirty student rooms. Admission is 20 dirhams, payable in cash.

to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through the medina of Fez: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walk of 0.1 km in 2 minutes is correct.

visits.text: The religious and scholarly heart of Fez since the 9th century, Al Quaraouiyine Mosque stands at the center of the medina. According to tradition, Fatima al-Fihri, the daughter of a wealthy merchant from Kairouan, Tunisia, founded it around 857 or 859. Al Quaraouiyine University grew around this mosque. Guinness World Records describes it as the oldest educational institution still operating in the world. The mosque is closed to non-Muslims. Through an open doorway, you can glimpse part of the courtyard: stay on the threshold and avoid prayer times.

to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through the medina of Fez: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walk of 0.1 km in 2 minutes is correct.

visits.text: The ringing of hammers on copper guides you to Seffarine Square. Its name means “coppersmiths,” the artisans who work copper. Their workshops were documented here as early as the 16th century. Even today, they hammer out large cauldrons here. Seffarine Madrasa, built in 1271, also opens onto the square: it is Morocco’s oldest building originally constructed as a madrasa. It still houses students and is not open to visitors. Settle beneath the old tree to watch the artisans, and ask before photographing a workshop.
