visits.text: Climb to the terrace of a leather shop for an overhead view of Chouara Tannery, the largest of Fez’s three tanneries. The hides first soak in white vats containing water, salt, lime, and pigeon droppings: the ammonia in the droppings softens the leather. They then move into the dye vats, with poppy red, indigo blue, or henna orange. Access to the terrace is free, but leave 10 to 20 dirhams if you do not buy anything. If someone tells you “the tannery is closed today,” it is a trick to take you elsewhere.

to_next_leg.road_type: Red petit taxi from the medina to Fez el-Jdid

visits.text: If you arrive early, you will have the gates of the Royal Palace of Fez, known as Dar al-Makhzen, almost to yourself. The palace covers 80 hectares, the equivalent of more than a hundred soccer fields. It is not open to visitors. Its seven gates on Place des Alaouites were built from 1969 to 1971. Their gilded bronze doors are covered in geometric patterns and framed by blue zellige and carved cedar. Photograph the gates, but not the guards, and do not get too close.

to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through the medina of Fez: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walk of 0.5 km in 7 minutes is correct.

visits.text: In the mid-15th century, the Jews of Fez settled beside the Royal Palace in the Mellah neighborhood. The word means “salty place,” perhaps because of a saltwater spring or a former salt warehouse. On Rue Bou Khessissat, opened in 1924, Jewish houses have balconies facing the street. The Ibn Danan Synagogue, dating from the late 17th century, reopened in 1999 after restoration. From its roof, you can see the white tombs of the Jewish cemetery. Admission prices vary: ask on arrival.

to_next_leg.road_type: On foot via Grande Rue de Fès el-Jdid
to_next_leg.justification: Trajet urbain fait à pied entre mellah fes et jnan sbil, environ 1100 m de marche réelle comptés 1 km : l'ancienne durée de 2 min venait du calcul voiture, elle est remplacée par 14 min de marche.

activities.text: Catch your breath in Jnan Sbil Garden, created in the 19th century by Sultan Moulay Hassan I. It lies between Fez el-Bali, “Old Fez,” and Fez el-Jdid, “New Fez,” built in the 13th century by the Marinids. Its 7.5 hectares, roughly the equivalent of ten soccer fields, were restored from 2006 to 2010 and reopened in 2011. You will find a large pool, a bamboo garden, and norias, the large wheels that draw water for irrigation. Al Batha Museum is then a 10-minute walk away.

practical_info.tip: Admission is free according to recent information. Allow 45 minutes to walk around the pool and the norias.

to_next_leg.road_type: On foot via Bab Boujloud, Batha
to_next_leg.justification: Trajet urbain fait à pied entre jnan sbil et musee al batha, environ 600 m de marche réelle comptés 1 km : l'ancienne durée de 2 min venait du calcul voiture, elle est remplacée par 9 min de marche.

visits.text: Al Batha Museum of Islamic Arts occupies Dar Batha Palace, the sultans’ summer residence in the late 19th century. Converted into a museum in 1915, it reopened on February 26, 2025, after six years of restoration. Among its roughly 700 works, look for the minbar from the Mosque of the Andalusians, a carved wooden pulpit more than a thousand years old from which the imam preaches. The Andalusian garden, designed in 1915, is divided into four sections around a fountain. Admission is 60 dirhams, with opening hours from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., except Tuesdays; allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

to_next_leg.road_type: Red petit taxi, about 10 dirhams

visits.text: Borj Nord kept watch over the enemies of Fez, as well as the city’s own inhabitants. Sultan Ahmed al-Mansour of the Saadian dynasty had this fort built in 1582 on a hill north of the medina. At the time, the people of Fez el-Bali were considered unruly, and the fort was also intended to keep them in check. Today, the fort houses an arms museum: cannons occupy two rooms, alongside sabers, daggers, and rifles. Look for the large firing platform, pierced with 56 openings for cannons. The museum is closed on Mondays.

to_next_leg.road_type: Short direct walk between two neighbouring sights
to_next_leg.justification: Trajet urbain fait à pied entre borj nord fes et tombeaux merinides fes, environ 750 m de marche réelle comptés 1 km : l'ancienne durée de 2 min venait du calcul voiture, elle est remplacée par 9 min de marche. Nom des rues empruntées non vérifié : la description du trajet reste volontairement générale.

visits.text: End the weekend on the hill of the Marinid Tombs, an eight-minute walk from Borj Nord. The entire medina of Fez stretches out before you, with its tightly packed houses and minarets. This 14th-century necropolis is attributed to the Marinids, the dynasty that built the Bou Inania and Al-Attarine madrasas. Two tall, ruined mausoleums with large horseshoe arches remain. Access is free, with no facilities: bring water. Come with others and take a petit taxi back down before nightfall, as thefts have been reported here in the evening.

seo.h1_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah
seo.intro_paragraph: This 2-day weekend in Fez takes you on foot through the medina, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981, and by petit taxi to Fez el-Jdid and the hills. The first day leads downhill from Bab Bou Jeloud to Chouara Tannery via the Bou Inania and Al-Attarine madrasas, the Nejjarine Museum, and Seffarine Square. The second connects the Royal Palace gates, the Mellah, Jnan Sbil Garden, Al Batha Museum, Borj Nord, and the Marinid Tombs.
seo.seo_hook: Fez in 2 days on foot: Bab Bou Jeloud, the Bou Inania and Al-Attarine madrasas, Chouara Tannery, the Mellah, Al Batha Museum, and the Marinid Tombs.

itineraries.title: High Atlas in 7 Days: Ourika, Imlil, Télouet, and Ouzoud
itineraries.subtitle: In 7 days, travel from Lake Lalla Takerkoust to Ouzoud Falls via Imlil, Tichka Pass, and the Ounila Valley.
itineraries.notes: The earthquake of September 8, 2023, struck Al Haouz Province: reconstruction continues around Imlil and Asni, and Tinmel Mosque, which is undergoing restoration, is not included in the itinerary. Drive during daylight hours on mountain roads, and check the weather in winter, as snow can close Tizi n’Tichka Pass from December to March.
itineraries.climate: Best times to visit: April–May and September–October, with afternoon temperatures of 26 to 33 °C in Marrakech and cool nights at higher elevations. Avoid July and August, when average afternoon temperatures in Marrakech exceed 37 °C and thunderstorms often develop in the mountains. From November to March, snow can close Tizi n’Tichka Pass, and January nights in Imlil can drop to around -2 °C.

activities.text: Leave Marrakech in the morning, heading southwest on the road to Amizmiz. This itinerary does not linger in the city, heading straight for the High Atlas Mountains. Lake Lalla Takerkoust, the first stop, is about 35 km away, a drive of 40 minutes to 1 hour depending on traffic. Fill up before leaving Marrakech and bring supplies for a picnic.

practical_info.tip: Pick up your rental car the day before or early in the morning to avoid traffic jams on the way out of Marrakech.

to_next_leg.road_type: Road southwest toward Amizmiz

visits.text: A broad expanse of water among dry hills, with the High Atlas peaks as a backdrop on clear days: this is Lake Lalla Takerkoust. It is an artificial reservoir. Its dam was built between 1929 and 1935, during the French protectorate, on the Oued N’Fis (oued means river). The water irrigates the Haouz Plain around Marrakech and is also used to generate electricity. Come before 9 a.m. or in the late afternoon, when the lake is calmer and the light on the mountains is softer.

If you have binoculars, follow the western shore of Lake Lalla Takerkoust, the best side for birdwatching. A narrow paved road runs for about 5 km along this shore, with several viewpoints along the way. During the spring and fall migrations, you may spot ruddy shelducks, reddish ducks; black-winged stilts, with their very long legs; or ospreys, birds of prey that dive for fish. Their numbers depend on the water level. A spotting scope makes observing them much easier.

activities.text: Swimming is officially prohibited in Lake Lalla Takerkoust, but you can still head out onto the water. Rental operators along the shore offer pedal boats, small motorboats, and Jet Skis. Some also advertise swimming areas: check the rules on-site before entering the water. The lake is calmer on weekdays. In summer, avoid midday, when the heat is intense and shade is scarce.

practical_info.tip: Save the late afternoon for watching the sunset over the lake before spending the night on its shore.

to_next_leg.road_type: Narrow road with switchbacks via Ouazguita

visits.text: Thirteen hairpin turns and a climb of about 750 m over 19 km: the road from Lake Lalla Takerkoust up to the Kik Plateau must be earned. It first crosses dry hills, then winds upward to an elevation of about 1,320 m. Stop at one of the final bends wherever the shoulder allows: the lake comes into view below. This climb is well known among cyclists, so take care on the curves.

Moulay Brahim overlooks the gorges that bear its name, along the road descending from the Kik Plateau toward Asni. This holy village is clustered around the mausoleum of Moulay Brahim and draws many visitors from Marrakech. The shrine is a place of prayer: view it from the lanes without trying to enter. Farther down, Asni holds its weekly souk on Saturdays. If you pass through that day, stop for 1 hour to browse the stalls.

activities.text: Park on the Kik Plateau and walk for 1 to 2 hours among wheat fields and villages. The earthen Berber houses follow the mountain slope and blend into it. On the paths, donkeys and mules remain the surest way to reach the hamlets. In spring, snowmelt brings the meadows into bloom. The villages are very modest: bring water and a picnic, and always ask before photographing anyone.

practical_info.tip: Spring is the best season to visit the plateau, when flowers cover the meadows.

to_next_leg.road_type: Mountain road via Moulay Brahim and Asni

visits.text: The most beautiful part of Imlil is not its main street, lined with outdoor gear shops, but the terraced orchards surrounding it. At an elevation of 1,740 m, the village is the usual starting point for climbing Toubkal, North Africa’s highest peak at 4,167 m. The September 2023 earthquake hit the valley hard, and reconstruction continues. Toward the end of the day, follow the small irrigation channels that water the terraces: they reveal how these slopes are farmed.

activities.text: Walk uphill from Imlil to the village of Tamatert, at 1,810 m, along a path lined with walnut, apple, and cherry trees. In the surrounding villages, each family tends a few walnut trees. Their walnuts have shells so hard that they are soaked in water for 1 or 2 days so they can be cracked cleanly. If you still have energy, continue to Tizi n’Tamatert Pass, at 2,272 m. Head back down before nightfall: the trails are not lit.

practical_info.tip: Tizi n’Tamatert Pass is about 460 m higher than the village of Tamatert: save it for a day when you feel fit.

to_next_leg.road_type: Mule trail through the Aït Mizane Valley

visits.text: House upon house, Aroumd rises on a large moraine spur—a mass of rocks and earth left behind by an ancient glacier. At about 1,900 m, it is the highest village in the Aït Mizane Valley, around forty minutes on foot from Imlil. Below, terraces irrigated for a very long time produce barley, corn, and vegetables. The narrow lanes all look alike, making it easy to get lost, so follow the main path or ask for directions.

activities.text: If your legs are up to it, climb from Aroumd to the shrine of Sidi Chamharouch, at 2,350 m, on the Toubkal trail. Allow about two hours for the ascent, with a steep first half, and three to four hours round-trip from Aroumd. You will know you have arrived when you see tea stalls beside the stream, near a small waterfall. The shrine is a pilgrimage site closed to non-Muslims: view it from a distance. A licensed guide is mandatory for this hike on the Toubkal trail.

practical_info.tip: Set out early with water and a warm layer: in the mountains, the temperature drops by about 1 °C for every 150 m of elevation gain, making the shrine about 4 °C cooler than Imlil.

to_next_leg.road_type: Via Asni and Tahannaout, then through the Ourika Valley
to_next_leg.justification: The detour is unavoidable: no road crosses the mountains between Imlil and the Ourika Valley. You have to head back down through Asni and Tahannaout, then climb up the valley; the route planner gives the same result (80 km).

visits.text: A contemporary art garden in the Ourika Valley may come as a surprise, but Anima Garden makes the combination work. Austrian artist André Heller opened it in 2016, 27 km south of Marrakech. Plan a round-trip drive from Setti Fatma to visit the garden. Across three hectares, ceramic sculptures and pools mingle with plantings, with the Atlas Mountains as a backdrop. Arrive when it opens, at 9 a.m., to enjoy the peace and quiet. Admission is around 140 dirhams per adult: check the price before you go.

activities.text: Setti Fatma’s first waterfall is only the beginning: the seven-waterfall hike takes more effort higher up. The village, deep in a gorge, is the last in the Ourika Valley accessible by paved road. A steep trail leads to the base of the first and largest waterfall in twenty minutes. Another ten minutes of almost vertical climbing brings you to a viewpoint with a refreshment stand. It takes another hour of effort to reach the highest waterfall. Avoid weekends and summer, when residents of Marrakech flock here.

practical_info.tip: You do not need a guide to reach the first waterfall. For the trail higher up, wear sturdy hiking shoes.

activities.text: In the Ourika Valley, a village’s name can tell you its market day: Tnine Ourika comes from tnine, meaning “Monday” in Arabic. This is where the valley’s large weekly souk takes place every Monday. Farther up the valley, Aghbalou hosts a smaller market on Thursdays. From Setti Fatma, plan to drive down the valley to reach these markets. If you are visiting on either day, set aside an hour to browse the stalls, preferably in the morning.

practical_info.tip: From late October to late November, the Safranière de l’Ourika, a garden where saffron is grown, displays the flowers in full bloom.

to_next_leg.road_type: Through the Ourika Valley, then along the N9 via Taddert to the pass
to_next_leg.justification: The detour is unavoidable: no road connects the Ourika Valley directly to the pass. You have to head back down the valley, then rejoin the N9. I am keeping the route planner’s distance (122 km), which is more accurate than 157 km, and a travel time of 165 minutes, equivalent to about 45 km/h on mountain roads.

visits.text: Tizi n’Tichka Pass was long listed at 2,260 m, but a GPS measurement taken in 2022 puts it at about 2,205 m. It remains the highest of North Africa’s major road passes. The French army laid out the road in the 1930s along an old caravan trail. Its name means “pass of the pastures” in Tamazight, the Berber language. On a clear day, the view stretches as far as Toubkal. From December to March, snow can close the road: check the weather before setting out.

activities.text: Stop in Taddert, a village beside the N9, roughly halfway between Marrakech and Ouarzazate. Travelers stop here for a bite to eat or to browse local crafts before tackling Tizi n’Tichka Pass. The road has been modernized and is much safer than it once was. The curves and trucks still demand attention: take a break here if you have been driving since morning.

practical_info.tip: The northern side of the pass is green, while the southern side is drier and rockier: the landscape changes within just a few kilometers.

to_next_leg.road_type: P1506 road toward Télouet

visits.text: Behind crumbling earthen walls, the kasbah of Télouet hides reception rooms adorned with zellige (mosaics of small glazed tiles), carved stucco (plaster sculpted in relief), and painted cedar ceilings. The Glaoui family began building it around 1860. In 1893, a snowstorm stranded the army of Sultan Hassan I nearby. Madani El Glaoui supplied the court for several weeks and later became grand vizier, the equivalent of a prime minister. Since the 2023 earthquake, only some of the rooms have been open to visitors, with a guide included in the admission ticket.

activities.text: Télouet’s salt mines partly explain the Glaoui family’s wealth. Their kasbah stood on one of the main caravan routes between Marrakech and the southern valleys on the edge of the Sahara. Salt traveled alongside other goods. Near the village, a salt mine is still operating and can be visited. Ask in the village or check with your kasbah guide for directions.

practical_info.tip: Nights are cool in Télouet, at around 1,800 m above sea level: bring a warm layer, even in spring and fall.

to_next_leg.road_type: P1506 road through the Ounila Valley

visits.text: Anemiter is worth stopping for: its ksar, a fortified village with earthen walls, is one of the best preserved in Morocco. It lies about 15 kilometers from Télouet, at the start of the Ounila Valley. The painter Jacques Majorelle stayed here in 1921. Park at the top of the village and walk down into the old ksar: the track leading to it is in poor condition.

Though half in ruins, Tamdaght’s kasbah served as the setting for a major scene in director Ridley Scott’s film Gladiator. From Anemiter, plan a round-trip drive through the Ounila Valley to reach Tamdaght. A kasbah is the fortified residence of a prominent family. This one belonged to the Glaoui family, as did the palace in Télouet. Some rooms are no longer accessible. There is no ticket booth or opening hours: knock on the door to ask to enter.

activities.text: You will then head down the Ounila Valley on the P1506, a paved road suitable for a regular car. For about 40 kilometers, the Ounila River traces a ribbon of green farmland between ocher canyons. This valley was a route for caravans carrying salt and goods from the Sahara. Look out for cave dwellings carved into the rock, which served as shelters during conflicts. Without stops, the most scenic stretch takes 1 hour 30 minutes to drive.

practical_info.tip: After heavy rain, check road conditions: some sections may require a 4x4.

to_next_leg.road_type: P1506 road via Tamdaght

visits.text: Aït Ben Haddou’s earthen houses rise in tiers up a hillside beside the Ounila River. This ksar, or fortified village, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987. Lawrence of Arabia and later Gladiator were filmed here. Climb to the fortified communal granary at the top, known as an agadir, where harvests were stored. Only a few families still live in the ksar. There is no official admission fee.

to_next_leg.road_type: Return to Télouet via the N9, then take the road to Demnate

visits.text: In Amazigh, the Berber language, Imi n’Ifri means “the mouth of the cave.” This natural bridge, 6 km east of Demnate, is what remains of an enormous cave, most of which has collapsed. Many birds nest in its vaulted ceiling. A trail with about 300 steps leads down to the bottom of the gorge and passes beneath the arch. This section is exposed and has no railing: you need to be sure-footed and comfortable with heights.

Demnate, a small town at the foot of the High Atlas, retains its old ramparts and its kasbah in the center. A large Jewish community lived here from the early 12th century until the late 1950s. It was known for its wine and leatherworking. Olive groves surround the town. If you visit on a Sunday, stop by the weekly souk, where you can find red clay pottery.

to_next_leg.road_type: Mountain road to Ouzoud

visits.text: You hear Ouzoud Falls before you see them: their roar rises from the gorge as soon as you reach the first viewpoints. The water drops about 110 m in several tiers before flowing into the gorge of the Oued el-Abid, the river below. A maintained trail from the village of Tanaghmeilt leads to the foot of the falls in 15 to 20 minutes. There is no official admission ticket. Arrive early in the morning: it gets very crowded in summer.

Ouzoud is thought to come from an Amazigh word meaning “olive,” and olive trees do indeed surround the falls. About ten small traditional olive oil mills still operate along the river. Stop at one on your way down to Ouzoud Falls: it is a chance to see an old-fashioned mill at work, just steps from the water.

activities.text: Climb into one of the small shared boats waiting at the foot of Ouzoud Falls. Local operators steer them across the pool to get as close as possible to the main falls. From below, you get a better sense of the water’s 110 m drop. There is a charge for the ride: agree on the price before boarding, and put your phone in a waterproof pouch.

practical_info.tip: At the foot of the falls, a natural pool offers a place to cool off in summer.

activities.text: If you encounter Barbary macaques around Ouzoud Falls, do not feed them. They are a protected species and the only monkeys living in the wild in Morocco. Feeding them disrupts their natural behavior. To watch them, follow the loop trail that crosses the river at the foot of the falls and takes about 1 hour. Keep your bags and food securely closed.

practical_info.tip: Bring sturdy walking shoes for the loop around the falls.

activities.text: The trail through the Oued el-Abid gorges is worth the effort: it takes you far from the crowds gathered near Ouzoud Falls. The falls plunge into these gorges, and the site is part of the M’Goun UNESCO Global Geopark. A geopark is an area recognized for the richness of its rocks and landscapes. These trails are less traveled than the area around the falls: go with a licensed local guide and plenty of water.

practical_info.tip: Spring is the best season: the falls are at their highest flow then.

activities.text: You will head back to Marrakech after spending the morning at Ouzoud Falls. The city is about 150 km away, a drive of 2 hours 30 minutes to 3 hours, or longer if traffic is heavy on the way into Marrakech. Leave Ouzoud in the early afternoon: you will arrive before dark and have time to return your rental car without rushing.

practical_info.tip: If your flight leaves that evening, allow plenty of extra time to reach Marrakech Menara Airport.

seo.h1_title: High Atlas in 7 Days: Ourika, Imlil, Télouet, and Ouzoud
seo.intro_paragraph: This 7-day road trip starts and ends in Marrakech, winding through the High Atlas and its valleys. You travel from Lake Lalla Takerkoust to the villages of Imlil and Aroumd, then from the Ourika Valley to Tizi n’Tichka Pass. The loop finishes with the kasbah of Télouet, the Ounila Valley, Aït Ben Haddou, and Ouzoud Falls.
seo.seo_hook: Lake Lalla Takerkoust, a hike to Aroumd, the waterfalls of Setti Fatma, the kasbah of Télouet, and Ouzoud Falls: a 7-day road trip through the High Atlas.

itineraries.title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens
itineraries.subtitle: Spend 3 days exploring the medina’s palaces and souks on foot and by petit taxi, then visit Majorelle Garden and the Menara Gardens.
itineraries.notes: To find everything open, start on a Sunday, Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday: Lazama Synagogue on day 1 does not welcome visitors during Shabbat, and on day 3, the Yves Saint Laurent Museum is closed on Wednesdays and Dar El Bacha on Mondays. Majorelle Garden and the Yves Saint Laurent Museum sell tickets online only, while admission to the palaces must be paid in cash.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: March through May and October–November, with average highs of 23 to 29 °C. Avoid June, July, and August: average highs range from 34 to 38 °C, and record temperatures approach 50 °C. In winter, days remain mild, around 19 to 21 °C, but nighttime temperatures drop to 6 to 8 °C: bring a jacket for evenings in Jemaa el-Fna Square.

visits.text: “The booksellers’ mosque”: that is what Koutoubia means, a name recalling the booksellers’ souk that once surrounded it. Its 77 m minaret, completed in the late 12th century, serves as a landmark in the medina. Each of its four faces has a different arrangement of decorative arches: walk around it to compare them. On the esplanade, you can see the foundations of an earlier mosque. It is believed to have been replaced around 1158 because it was incorrectly aligned toward Mecca. The mosque is closed to non-Muslims: you can view the exterior free of charge.

to_next_leg.road_type: On foot via Rue Sidi Mimoun
to_next_leg.justification: Trajet urbain fait à pied entre mosquee koutoubia et bab agnaou, environ 1050 m de marche réelle comptés 1 km : l'ancienne durée de 2 min venait du calcul voiture, elle est remplacée par 13 min de marche.

visits.text: Carved shells frame the arch of Bab Agnaou, cut from ocher-colored sandstone. Completed around 1190 under the Almohad caliph Yacoub al-Mansour, this gate was the main entrance to the royal kasbah, the sultan’s citadel. Above the arch runs a frieze in Kufic script, an angular form of Arabic calligraphy, featuring verses from the Quran. The meaning of its Berber name remains debated. Stop on the outside to read the frieze, then pass through the gate: the Saadian Tombs are a five-minute walk away.

to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through the Marrakech medina: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walk of 0.3 km in 5 minutes is correct.

visits.text: If you arrive at the Saadian Tombs when they open, around 9 a.m., you will have a shorter wait to see the Hall of the Twelve Columns. This royal necropolis was built primarily by Sultan Ahmed al-Mansour, who died in 1603. His tomb lies in this hall, beneath twelve columns of Carrara marble, a white marble from Italy. Later, Sultan Moulay Ismaïl walled up most of the entrances. The French historic monuments service rediscovered the site in 1917, then opened it to the public. The rooms are viewed from behind barriers. Admission is 100 dirhams, payable in cash.

to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through the Marrakech medina: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walk of 0.8 km in 12 minutes is correct.

visits.text: Badi means “the Incomparable,” yet all that remains of this palace are immense earthen walls surrounding pools and gardens. Sultan Ahmed al-Mansour began building it in 1578. He likely financed it with the ransom paid by Portugal, which Morocco defeated that year. The Italian marble used for the columns was traded for its weight in sugar. Around 1707, Sultan Moulay Ismaïl had the palace dismantled to reuse its materials in Meknes. Damaged by the 2023 earthquake, the site reopened as early as October. Admission is 100 dirhams, payable in cash.

to_next_leg.road_type: Via Place des Ferblantiers
to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through the Marrakech medina: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walk of 0.4 km in 6 minutes is correct.

visits.text: The Mellah, Marrakech’s former Jewish quarter, begins at Place des Ferblantiers. Artisans still make metal lanterns by hand in this square. The neighborhood emerged in the mid-16th century, next to the royal kasbah. It had around 40,000 residents in the late 1940s. Today, around 200 Jews remain in Marrakech. In the narrow streets east of the main street, look for the small Stars of David on doors and grilles. The neighborhood is free to explore: ask before photographing residents.

activities.text: Shop for spices at the Mellah’s covered market, where stalls display ground spices in tall pyramids. The secret behind these perfect cones is a metal mold hidden inside. Look for ras el-hanout, a spice blend whose recipe varies from shop to shop. It often contains white pepper, ginger, turmeric, and cumin. Cumin is the main spice grown around Marrakech: choose round seeds, a sign of quality.

practical_info.tip: Spices and traditional cosmetics are often cheaper here than in the heart of the souks. Compare two or three stalls before buying.

to_next_leg.justification: The two sites are just a short walk apart in the Marrakech medina: the routing engine returned a null value; the current walk of 0.2 km in 4 minutes is correct.

visits.text: The Mellah’s loveliest surprise is hidden behind an unmarked door: Lazama Synagogue (Slat al-Azama). According to tradition, it was founded in 1492 by Jews expelled from Spain. A courtyard tiled in blue and white leads to the prayer hall. There, zellij mosaics made from glazed terra-cotta tiles form a Star of David. The rooms around the courtyard tell the story of Jewish life in Morocco. Visit Sunday through Thursday: during Shabbat, access is reserved for worshippers.

to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through the Marrakech medina: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walk of 0.5 km in 7 minutes is correct.

visits.text: More than 20,000 whitewashed graves cover Miâara Jewish Cemetery, the largest in Morocco. Near the entrance, some graves are painted blue. These belong to the Cohanim, descendants of the priests of the Temple in Jerusalem. Men, women, and children are buried in separate sections. One corner of the cemetery holds around 6,000 children who died during a typhus epidemic in the 19th century. Men are lent a kippah at the entrance, and a donation to the caretaker is customary. Avoid Saturdays and Jewish holidays.

Look up in every room of Bahia Palace, whose name means “the Brilliant”: its painted cedar ceilings are the highlight of the visit. Grand Vizier Si Moussa, the sultan’s prime minister, began construction in the 1860s. His son Ba Ahmed expanded it until 1900, bringing the palace to around 150 rooms. The grand courtyard, measuring 50 m by 30 m, is paved with Carrara marble. Damaged by the 2023 earthquake, the palace is still undergoing restoration. Open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.; admission is 100 dirhams, payable in cash.

to_next_leg.road_type: On foot via Rue Riad Zitoun el Jdid
to_next_leg.justification: Trajet urbain fait à pied entre palais de la bahia et place jemaa el fna, environ 1050 m de marche réelle comptés 1 km : l'ancienne durée de 5 min venait du calcul voiture, elle est remplacée par 13 min de marche.

visits.text: Jemaa el-Fna square changes throughout the day. In the morning, orange juice vendors, snake charmers, and artists working with henna, a plant-based dye applied to the skin, set up in the half-empty square. Around 4 p.m., cooks assemble their stalls. At sunset, musicians and Berber troupes draw crowds, often until around 1 a.m. In 2001, UNESCO recognized the square for its storytellers and street performers. For a view of it all from above, head to a café terrace at the edge of the square.

activities.text: Have dinner on the benches at Jemaa el-Fna’s food stalls, which light up as night falls. Try snail soup, skewers, tagine, or fried fish. Choose a busy stall, eat with bread instead of utensils, and drink bottled water. Arrive early in the evening to find a seat. The French Ministry for Foreign Affairs reports bag and phone thefts in Marrakech: keep your valuables close to you.

practical_info.tip: A tip is expected if you photograph a musician, storyteller, or snake charmer.

activities.text: The best part of Marrakech’s souks is wandering without a particular destination. Start at the northeast corner of Jemaa el-Fna and head up to Souk Semmarine, the main covered passageway. Its slatted roof, once made of reeds, is now metal to reduce the risk of fire. Farther along, the passage branches off toward other souks, each originally associated with a trade: leather, metalwork, jewelry, or carpets. Bargain with a smile, but never go back on an agreed price.

practical_info.tip: To find your way, ask shopkeepers rather than the young people offering to guide you, often for a fee. Official guides carry a professional ID card.

to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through the Marrakech medina: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walk of 0.2 km in 3 minutes is correct.

activities.text: Cumin, saffron, and paprika add color to the stalls of Rahba Kedima, a small, sunny square amid the souks. It is also known as Spice Square. Shops around its edges sell spices, traditional cosmetics, and herbal remedies. Some offerings are surprising, such as dried lizards. In the center, women sell woven baskets and cotton caps. Several cafés line the square, making it an ideal place to take a breather away from the narrow passageways.

practical_info.tip: Compare prices with those you saw the day before at the Mellah market, where spices are often cheaper.

to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through the Marrakech medina: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walk of 0.4 km in 6 minutes is correct.

visits.text: If you visit the dyers’ souk before noon, you will see artisans working over their vats. Skeins, those long loops of wool, dry above the alley in yellow, blue, or red. Natural colors come from saffron, indigo, poppies, or cochineal, a small insect that is crushed. Many workshops now use chemical dyes. Admission is free: turn down anyone claiming that a guide is required. A close-up photo of an artisan often costs 10 to 20 dirhams.

to_next_leg.justification: The two places are just a few steps apart in the Marrakech medina: the routing engine returned a null value; the current walk of 0.15 km in 3 minutes is correct.

visits.text: In 2000, the grounds of Le Jardin Secret were just a pile of rubble divided among more than 130 owners. Yet in the 19th century, one of the medina’s largest riads—houses built around an interior garden—stood here. Caid U-Bihi, a powerful local leader, had it built. Restored with private funding, the site opened to the public in 2016. English landscape designer Tom Stuart-Smith created two gardens here: an Islamic garden with geometric paths lined with citrus trees, and an exotic garden arranged around a large jacaranda tree. Admission is 100 dirhams, free for children under 12.

activities.text: Climb to the top of the tower at Le Jardin Secret for a view over the medina’s rooftops. On your way down, follow the channels and pools in the Islamic garden. They were supplied by khettaras, underground tunnels dug to bring groundwater into the city. These old channels have been restored. The tower ticket costs 40 dirhams in addition to admission. Children under 6 are not allowed in the tower.

practical_info.tip: Open daily from 9:30 a.m. Closes at 5:30 p.m. in November and December, 6 p.m. in October, 6:30 p.m. from January to March, and 7:30 p.m. from April to September.

visits.text: Ben Youssef Madrasa, a former Quranic school that housed students, is the largest in Morocco. The Saadian sultan Abdallah al-Ghalib completed it in 1564–1565. Its 130 rooms surround a courtyard where a shallow pool reflects the carved facades. The school could accommodate up to 800 students. Head upstairs to see how cramped the rooms are, with light coming in from the courtyard. Closed in 2018 for restoration, the madrasa reopened in April 2022. It is open daily from 9 AM to 7 PM; admission is 50 dirhams.

to_next_leg.justification: The two sites are just steps apart in the Marrakech medina: the routing engine returned a null value; the current walk of 0.25 km in 4 minutes is correct.

visits.text: There are no palaces or gardens here, but faces: the Maison de la Photographie showcases photographs of Morocco dating back to the 1870s. Two collectors, Parisian Patrick Menac’h and Marrakech native Hamid Mergani, assembled these vintage prints. Portraits fill the ground floor. Near the rooftop, a documentary about the High Atlas, filmed by Daniel Chicault in 1956, is screened. Finish on the terrace with a juice or coffee overlooking the rooftops. Open from 9:30 AM to 7 PM; admission is 50 dirhams.

visits.text: To enjoy Majorelle Garden before the crowds, book the first time slot at 8 AM: the site receives more than 700,000 visitors a year. Painter Jacques Majorelle began creating this garden in 1923 and opened it to the public in 1947. He gave his name to Majorelle blue, the intense cobalt blue that covers his villa. Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé bought and restored the property in the 1980s. The fashion designer’s ashes were scattered here in 2008. Tickets are sold exclusively online through the garden’s official website.

The Pierre Bergé Museum of Berber Arts occupies Jacques Majorelle’s former painting studio in the heart of the garden. Opened in 2011, it introduces the Amazigh, the name the Berbers use for themselves, a people who have lived in North Africa for millennia. Its galleries span the Rif to the Sahara, displaying jewelry, clothing, weapons, carved doors, rugs, and musical instruments. One section also explores Berber Jews. Museum admission is separate from garden admission: add it when booking. Open from 8:30 AM to 5 PM.

visits.text: Seen from the street, the facade of the Yves Saint Laurent Museum resembles fabric: its terracotta bricks form a woven pattern. Designed by the French firm Studio KO, the building opened in October 2017, just steps from Majorelle Garden. The permanent gallery displays around fifty haute couture pieces. They are rotated regularly to preserve them. The museum is open from 10 AM to 6 PM and closed on Wednesdays. Book a combined ticket with the garden on the official website.

visits.text: In 1910, Thami El Glaoui, the future pasha of Marrakech, meaning the city’s governor, commissioned Dar El Bacha. He wanted it to be luxurious enough to impress his guests. Since 2017, the palace has housed the Museum of Confluences, dedicated to Moroccan decorative arts and objects from other cultures. Its exhibitions change regularly. Damaged by the 2023 earthquake, the museum reopened as early as November of that year. It is open Tuesday through Sunday from 10 AM to 6 PM and closed on Mondays. Expect to pay around 60 dirhams.

activities.text: Extend your visit at Bacha Coffee, the café set in a historic salon at Dar El Bacha. This café specializes in arabica, a variety of coffee bean. Reservations are not accepted, and a line may form at busy times. Coffee is charged separately, in addition to museum admission.

practical_info.tip: Then take a petit taxi to the Menara Gardens: agree on the fare before getting in.

to_next_leg.road_type: Petit taxi, with the fare agreed on before getting in

visits.text: Do not come to the Menara Gardens expecting flower beds: this is a vast olive grove surrounding a pool, with a single, beautiful view. The pavilion with its green tile roof, completed in 1870, is reflected in the water, with the Atlas Mountains in the background on clear days. The pool, built in the 12th century, is elevated, allowing water to flow down to the olive trees by gravity. The water comes from the Atlas Mountains through khettaras, underground tunnels. Admission to the garden is free; the pavilion costs 60 dirhams.

seo.h1_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day stay in Marrakech takes you on foot through the medina, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985. The first day leads from the Koutoubia to the palaces, the Mellah, and Jemaa el-Fna square; the second takes you to the souks, Le Jardin Secret, and Ben Youssef Madrasa. On the third day, a petit taxi takes you to Majorelle Garden, the Yves Saint Laurent Museum, Dar El Bacha, and then the Menara Gardens.
seo.seo_hook: Koutoubia, Bahia Palace, the Saadian Tombs, the souks, Ben Youssef Madrasa, and Majorelle Garden: Marrakech in 3 days, on foot and by petit taxi.

itineraries.title: Northern Morocco in 6 Days: Asilah, Tetouan, and Al Hoceima
itineraries.subtitle: Spend 6 days following Morocco’s northern coast from Asilah to Al Hoceima, via Lixus, Tetouan, and the road through the Rif.
itineraries.notes: In the Rif, France Diplomatie advises driving during daylight hours and avoiding stops on secondary roads; after heavy rain, landslides sometimes block the N16 between Oued Laou and Al Hoceima, with a detour through Chefchaouen. Al Hoceima Airport has connections to Casablanca, Tangier, and Tetouan, along with a few direct flights to Brussels, Amsterdam, or Rotterdam: check these flights before renting a car to drop off in Al Hoceima.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May–June and September–October, with highs of 22 to 27 °C in Tangier. July and August are hotter (28 to 29 °C), and the beaches are packed, though the sea reaches 23 °C in Al Hoceima. Avoid November through January: Tangier receives more than 100 mm of rain per month, and landslides can close the coastal road through the Rif.

activities.text: Pick up your rental car at Tangier Ibn Battouta Airport, southwest of the city. Tangier deserves a trip of its own: on this itinerary, its airport serves only as the starting point for the Atlantic coast. Before signing the rental agreement, ask how much it costs to drop off the car in Al Hoceima. The route ends nearly 300 km from Tangier, on the Mediterranean.

practical_info.tip: Keep some cash in dirhams for admission to the day’s sites, which you often pay on arrival.

visits.text: In 1904, the kidnapping of an American in this forest brought the United States Navy to Tangier. Perdicaris Park bears his name: Ion Perdicaris had a villa here, where tribal chief Raissouni kidnapped him on May 18, 1904. President Roosevelt sent seven warships to Tangier, and the hostage was released for a ransom. Since 2022, the restored villa has housed a heritage interpretation center. Afterward, take a walk through Rmilat Forest, overlooking the Strait of Gibraltar.

Cape Spartel marks the point where the Atlantic Ocean meets the Mediterranean Sea, 14 km west of Tangier. Its lighthouse was built in 1864 at the request of European consuls concerned about the many shipwrecks offshore. In 1865, ten foreign countries and Morocco signed an agreement to maintain it jointly. On a clear day, look across the water for Cape Trafalgar on the Spanish coast, 44 km away.

An opening onto the ocean traces the outline of Africa: this is the sight visitors come to see at the Caves of Hercules. Waves carved out these caves, and local people later enlarged them by cutting out millstones for oil presses. According to legend, Hercules rested here before going to pick the golden apples in the Garden of the Hesperides. The ground is dark and slippery: wear sturdy shoes, and come early or in the late afternoon to avoid the crowds.

Few Moroccan medinas are as peaceful as Asilah’s. A medina is a fortified old town, and this one is entirely pedestrian. Its ramparts were built by the Portuguese, who captured the city on August 24, 1471. Enter through Bab al-Homer, the Land Gate, and leave through Bab al-Bahr, the Sea Gate. Right beside it, Borj al-Bahr, a bastion completed in 1516, projects into the ocean.

Borj al-Kamra, the main tower in Asilah’s ramparts, rises above Sidi Ali ben Hamdouch Square. It dates to 1509. The Portuguese called it Torre de Menagem, meaning the keep: the strongest tower, where people retreated during an attack. Walk around this massive square structure, then use the square as a meeting point that is easy to find in the medina.

The walls of Asilah’s medina are white, but their appearance changes every year. Since 1978, the Asilah International Cultural Moussem, a festival founded by painter Mohamed Melehi and mayor Mohamed Benaïssa, has had new murals painted on houses each year. The festival includes a summer session and a fall session, with concerts and exhibitions depending on the program. Wander without a route in mind, camera in hand: every alley may reveal a recent mural.

A former bandit had this palace built beside the ocean. Raissouni Palace dates to 1909 and is named after Moulay Ahmed er-Raissouni, the tribal chief who had kidnapped Ion Perdicaris five years earlier. Its reception room combines zellige (a mosaic of small glazed tiles), stucco (carved plasterwork), and painted wood. A terrace overlooks the ocean. Now a cultural center, it opens for exhibitions and events during the Cultural Moussem: at other times, view its facade from the ramparts.

Tombs covered in colorful ceramics descend toward the ocean in Asilah’s seaside cemetery. Walk discreetly along the edge of this Muslim cemetery, without walking between the graves. The overlook above it offers an unobstructed view of the setting sun, with the Atlantic as a backdrop. Arrive half an hour before sunset to find a good spot.

activities.text: If Asilah’s main beach feels too urban, drive south to Rmilat Beach, nicknamed Paradise Beach. This 5 km stretch of sand is wilder than the town beach. The official beach information sheet lists no drinking water supply, so bring water and a beach umbrella.

practical_info.tip: In summer, the official beach survey records up to 15,000 people per day: come in the morning.

visits.text: On the hill of Lixus, 80 m above the Loukkos River, the Phoenicians built a city in the 8th and 7th centuries BCE. These seafarers came from present-day Lebanon. Follow the path to the temple district, the largest excavated area of the site. The city’s economy depended on salted fish, shipped in amphorae—large earthenware jars whose fragments can still be found. The site is open daily from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., and admission costs 80 dirhams for a foreign adult.

Pliny the Elder, a Roman scholar of the 1st century, placed the Garden of the Hesperides, guarded by a dragon, at Lixus. To him, this dragon was simply a metaphor for the Loukkos River, which snakes across the plain in broad loops. Start at the interpretation center, opened in 2019, where panels help make sense of the rather inconspicuous ruins. Then head uphill to look at the river’s meanders: you will see Pliny’s dragon.

White facades and café terraces: Liberation Square is the lively heart of Larache. The Spanish occupied the city twice, from 1610 to 1689 and then from 1911 to 1956. During the protectorate, they named this square Plaza de España. Its Arab-Andalusian style recalls nearby Andalusia. Have a coffee at an outdoor table and watch the city go about its day.

Pass through Bab el-Medina, the gate opening onto the square, to enter Larache’s medina. Souk Esseghir, the small market, leads to narrow streets that descend to the fishing port. Then return to the central market, 200 m from the square, a renovated covered building in the Andalusian style. Go during the day, when the stalls are at their liveliest.

If you could take away just one view of Larache, it would be the one from Balcon Atlantique. This viewpoint, whose name means “balcony over the Atlantic,” overlooks the ocean. Travel guides rank it among the city’s finest views. Come at the end of the day to watch the sun set over the sea, then walk back to the center.

French writer Jean Genet is buried in Larache’s old Spanish cemetery, at the end of the waterfront promenade. He had lived here for several years and asked to be buried here; he died in 1986. Spanish writer Juan Goytisolo, who died in 2017, is buried in the same cemetery. Be discreet: this is a place for quiet reflection, with no visitor facilities.

activities.text: End the day at Larache’s fishing port, below the medina. The fish landed here help give the city its reputation, along with the region’s oranges and berries. Choose a simple local eatery and ask for the day’s fish, grilled. Confirm the price by weight before it is cooked.

practical_info.tip: Fish is often priced by weight: have it weighed in front of you.

map_keywords: Bab El Okla Ethnographic Museum Tétouan

visits.text: Small but complete: that is how UNESCO describes Tetouan’s World Heritage–listed medina. After the Reconquista, the reconquest of Spain by Christian monarchs, refugees expelled from Andalusia rebuilt the city. A wall roughly 5 km long surrounds it, with seven gates. Follow the main streets connecting these gates: they lead to squares, mosques, and artisan quarters. An official guide will save you unnecessary detours.

Smaller and less colorful than those in Fez, Tetouan’s tanneries make no attempt to impress. A tannery is a workshop where animal hides are processed into leather in vats. This one dates to the late 15th or early 16th century. Look for the small door to the left of Bab Mkabar, one of the medina’s gates, and keep a few dirhams handy for a tip.

“The cleanest and best built”: that was explorer Charles de Foucauld’s assessment of Tetouan’s mellah in 1883. A mellah is the former Jewish quarter of a Moroccan city. This one had as many as six thousand Jewish residents in the late 19th century. Look for its houses with second-floor balconies and paired pointed-arch windows, which distinguish it from the rest of the medina.

An old bastion, a defensive structure built around 1830 above the Bab el-Okla gate, houses Tetouan’s ethnographic museum. It reopened in January 2022. Ethnography studies ways of life: here, clothing, jewelry, and instruments tell the story of daily life in the city. One room presents the squndo, a 15th-century water distribution network that served the medina. Finish in the small garden, with views of the city and the Rif Mountains.

Step inside the School of Arts and Crafts, just outside Bab el-Okla. Founded in 1919 under the Spanish protectorate, it trains artisans in Moroccan and Andalusian crafts. Since 1928, it has occupied a richly decorated building surrounded by a garden. Visit Monday through Friday, as the school does not receive visitors on weekends; on Fridays, it takes a long midday break.

If Lixus left you wanting more, Tetouan’s archaeological museum rounds out the visit. It displays mosaics, Latin inscriptions, and amphorae from Lixus and Tamuda, another ancient city in the region. A scale model depicts the M’Zora cromlech, a circle of large standing stones in northern Morocco. The museum is open Wednesday through Monday; allow time for its Arab-Andalusian garden.

The Ensanche, the new town built by the Spanish west of the medina, is a reminder that Tetouan was the capital of the Spanish protectorate from 1913 to 1956. Residents call it Chanti. Its five-story buildings have stores on the ground floor. The Church of Our Lady of Victories, consecrated in 1925, dominates Moulay el-Mehdi Square. Finish on pedestrian-only Mohammed V Avenue, where cafés and used-book sellers bring the street to life in the evening.

Trains no longer stop at Tetouan’s old station, yet people still come through its doors. The Modern Art Center has occupied the building since 2013. It mainly showcases contemporary Moroccan and Andalusian artists, and its temporary exhibitions can be worth a detour. Admission is free. It is open Tuesday through Saturday, with a midday break: come in the morning or late afternoon.

activities.text: Crisp on the outside and fragrant with lemon inside: that is Tetouan-style pastilla. Pastilla is an oven-baked pie made with very thin sheets of dough and a meat filling. In Tetouan, it is prepared with chicken, eggs, and lemon. Order it at a restaurant in the medina and share it with a group, as it is filling.

practical_info.tip: Pastilla is eaten hot: ask whether it is made to order.

activities.text: In summer, Martil Beach receives up to 80,000 people a day, according to the official beach survey. This seaside resort is the closest to Tetouan, northeast of the city. Its sand stretches for 4 km to the mouth of the Martil River, which the Spanish called Río Martín. Walk along the waterfront, then rejoin the coastal road heading southeast.

practical_info.tip: In July and August, come early in the morning to find a spot on the sand.

to_next_leg.road_type: N16 coastal road, then P4105 through the valley

visits.text: A vertical rock face, carved into strange shapes, borders the river at the bottom of the Oued Laou gorges. The valley is part of Talassemtane National Park, established in 2004. Since 2006, the park has also been part of a UNESCO biosphere reserve, a protected area spanning Morocco and Spain. Barbary macaques, tailless monkeys classified as endangered, frequent these cliffs. Keep your distance and never feed them.

activities.text: Head up the valley on the P4105, a paved road with little traffic, stopping on the shoulders to look at the river. The Moroccan firs that are the park’s reason for being grow much higher up, at elevations between 1,400 and 2,000 m. Here, you are exploring the lower part of the park, shaped by water. The park covers nearly 60,000 hectares, almost six times the area of Paris. Turn back whenever you like to spend the night in Oued Laou.

practical_info.tip: Drive during daylight and park only on wide shoulders, never on a curve.

to_next_leg.road_type: P4105 through the Oued Laou valley

visits.text: Five kilometers of sand between the mountain and the sea: welcome to Oued Laou Beach. The town, 44 km from Tetouan, relies mainly on fishing outside the summer season. In summer, vacationers arrive and festivities bring the town to life. Walk along the sand to the river mouth, where the Oued Laou River flows into the sea.

activities.text: The best meal in Oued Laou is a plate of grilled sardines. The Moon guide describes this fishing port as a quiet town where people eat sardines and tagines. Settle into a small restaurant near the port and ask for the catch of the day. On Saturday, browse the souk, the weekly outdoor market.

practical_info.tip: The souk takes place on Saturdays: plan your stop around that day if possible.

to_next_leg.road_type: N16 coastal road, many curves

visits.text: El Jebha means “the forehead” in Arabic: the Rif Mountains frame this small port like a forehead above the sea. Under the Spanish protectorate, the town was called Puerto Capaz. Its port shelters many fishing boats and also welcomes recreational boaters cruising along the coast. Walk around the docks before getting back on the road.

activities.text: If you pass through on a Tuesday, stop at El Jebha’s souk, one of the largest and liveliest in the region according to the Moon guide. A souk is a traditional market. On other days, head down to the 1.8 km sand-and-pebble beach at the mouth of the Ouringa, a small river. There are no showers or restrooms: bring water.

practical_info.tip: The souk takes place on Tuesdays.

to_next_leg.road_type: N16 mountain road, then a descent to the coast

visits.text: Five watchtowers, attributed to the Portuguese by the Moroccan National Tourist Office, gave the village of Torres de Alcala its name. Torres means “towers” in Spanish. You are in Al Hoceima National Park, established in 2004, which protects 50 km of coastline and part of the sea. Climb up to the ruins for a view of the bay, then head down to the pebble-and-sand beach at the mouth of the Beni Boufrah River.

A rocky islet 500 m offshore encloses the bay of Cala Iris, a few kilometers to the west. The small port shelters around thirty fishing boats. The islet is part of the national park: it is one of the few places where the ferruginous limpet, an endangered shellfish that clings to rocks, survives. Do not collect anything from the rocks, and swim at the beach of sand mixed with pebbles.

activities.text: If you still have energy, follow the coastal trail east from Cala Iris. Reaching the area around Peñón de Vélez de la Gomera requires a long hike: allow enough time for the round trip. This rock has belonged to Spain since 1564. In 1930, an earthquake connected it to the coast with an 85 m sandbar. Directly opposite stood Badis, the port that served the inland city of Fez from the 14th to the 16th century. If you do not have enough time for the round trip, walk along the trail for 30 minutes to enjoy the coastal views, then retrace your steps.

practical_info.tip: Bring water and a hat: the coastal trail is exposed to the sun.

to_next_leg.road_type: Mountain road, then the N16 toward Al Hoceima

visits.text: Al Hoceima is a young city: the Spanish founded it in the 1920s under the name Villa Sanjurjo. A Catholic church from the colonial era still stands in the center. Spanish remains widely spoken here. In the evening, head to Mohammed VI Square. Its ground-level fountains light up at nightfall.

Walk down to Quemado Beach, a few minutes from central Al Hoceima. This is the city beach, just 300 m long. In summer, pedal boats are available for rent, and the beach fills up very quickly. In the off-season, you are more likely to see fishermen bringing in their catch. Come early in the morning to enjoy it while it is quiet.

The best time to stroll around Al Hoceima’s port is late in the day. The Moroccan tourist office recommends walking here to watch the fishermen at work. It is the Rif’s second port after Nador. Ferries also connect it to Motril, Spain. Watch out for ropes and crates: this is a working port, not a marina.

The sand at Sfiha Beach is black, and three islets dot the horizon. One of them, Peñón de Alhucemas, has a fortress and remains under Spanish sovereignty. The 2 km beach belongs to the municipality of Ajdir, the birthplace of Abdelkrim el-Khattabi. This leader from the Rif fought the Spanish army and proclaimed the Republic of the Rif in 1921. In summer, the official count records up to 10,000 swimmers a day: come early.

If Quemado is packed, head to Cala Bonita, another of the city’s beaches. This cove is tucked into a bay enclosed by rocky cliffs. Access is down a few steps, making it less convenient with a stroller. Bring water and a beach umbrella, and arrive early to choose your spot.

activities.text: After 6 p.m., buy your fish directly from the boats docked at Al Hoceima’s port. Then have it grilled at the Club nautique restaurant, the best-known restaurant in the port. Its upper floor overlooks the entire port, making it an ideal place to end the trip in peace. Ask how much grilling costs before ordering.

practical_info.tip: Choose a whole fish with bright eyes: this is a sign that it has just been caught.

activities.text: The coastline of Al Hoceima National Park is best seen from the sea. Small boats leave the port to cruise along the coast. The park is home to a large concentration of ospreys, large birds of prey that dive to catch fish. Negotiate the price and duration before boarding, and bring a windbreaker.

practical_info.tip: Trips depend on sea conditions: check at the port the day before.

seo.h1_title: Northern Morocco in 6 Days: Asilah, Tetouan, and Al Hoceima
seo.intro_paragraph: This 6-day road trip starts in Tangier and follows the Atlantic coast to Asilah and the ruins of Lixus. It then reaches the Mediterranean via the medina of Tetouan before following the Rif coastal road to Al Hoceima National Park. Along the way, you explore medinas, ancient sites, gorges, and coves.
seo.seo_hook: The Caves of Hercules, Asilah’s murals, the ruins of Lixus, Tetouan’s medina, and Al Hoceima’s coves: 6 days on Morocco’s northern coast.
featured_list: Cape Spartel: an 1864 lighthouse and the Caves of Hercules facing the strait
Asilah: a pedestrian medina within Portuguese ramparts dating from 1471
Lixus: a Phoenician hilltop site above the bends of the Loukkos River
Tetouan: a UNESCO-listed medina, mellah, and Bab el-Okla Museum
Al Hoceima National Park: the towers of Torres de Alcala and Cala Iris Bay
